The London Omnibus.—Many curious suFfestions have been made for the solution of the London street traffic problem, and amongst these must be classed the idea of running omnibuses "for men only." Elderly women it is true, usually stop omnibuses for getting on or alighting, and so do elderly men, but young women are fully expected to jump off and on without stopping the vehicle. The art of doing this successfully is, in fact, a necessity for all girls who use the London obni- buses. Conductors are supposed to stop if requested, but they generally look at any young woman who insists upon this,—and as much as fell her that what she wants is not a bus but a bathchair.—Not that conductors or drivers are less polite than they formerly were. On the contrary they have improved, and one very seldom hears the coarse language and abuse in the streets, for which this class of men used to be notorious. Their wit is not always in the best of taste, but it is often unmistakable as was that of the omnibus driver whose recollections evidently went back to 1670-71, and who remarked of a motor which was blocking the fray at the French Embassy, that "that would not be very tender eating at the next siege." Shopkeepers' Commissions.—lt is a very unpleasant development of modern competition in trade that people should be invited to accept commission for "puffing " certain goods to their friends. Apparently this method of business is found to pay, for there are always adver- tisements in the London papers offering inducements to people moving in good society to take such offices, but it is becerning pretty generallyknown that such methods are being adopted, and the people who are found to be recommending the goodsof particular firms will be sent to Coventry. Judicious people will very soon hesitate to advise the purchase of any. particular commodity, lest they should meet the experience of a benevolent old gentleman who, urging upon a rude youth the precious-. ness of time, was interrupted with an inquiry whether his counsellor wanted to sell him a watch.

Redeeming our Character.—Some three hundred em- ployees of the Sonvre stores—the famous Parisian em- porium—paid a visit to London at Whitsuntide, and let us hope their coming will further strengthen the Anglo- French entente. Unfortunately holiday time is not the best to see the fashionable side of the Metropolis, and possibly some of these visitors—all experts in the matter of dress—have gone back confirmed in the old belief that we are still lacking in decent attire and decent manners. If so it will be quite a wrong im- pression. as, for style in dress, London will now com- pare favourably with Paris, Vienna, or New York. Formerly we were supposed to combine a visit to

div.p: --- --- RHEUMATISM CURD,

At last it seems safe to say that a perfectly satisfac- tory cure for Rheumatism has been discovered. This remedy is called Dodd's Kidney Pills, and it has already- been tested in many very severe cases with the best re- sults. It is a specific medicine for the Kidneys, and the wonderful work it does in curing Rheumatism, Gout and such diseases is said to be due to the elimina- tion from the system of all uric acid, which is the cause of Rheumatism and kindred diseases. Many cases might be quoted in which this remedy has wrought perfect and permanent cures. For instance, Mr. I'. Frost, Neasby-road, Gipsy-lane,Belgr Leices- ter, has furnished the following facts "I had Rheumatism very badly, with cramps in muhcles and stiffness in the joints, my limbs would swell occasionally. I was treated by a doctor but got no better until a friend of mine advised me to try Dodd's Kidney Pills. I did qo and I am pleased to say that they did their work well, for which lam very thankful. lam recommending them everywhere I go as a cure for Rheumatism, for they are worth it." Mr. Frost's case is only one of many of thesame kind in which Dodd's Kidney Pills "have done their work well."

Methods of American political propaganda are some- times to say the least of it. peculiar. Thus we are told that last week a troupe of" minstrels" took up their position in front of the Capitol. at Washington and commenced a weird performance with their backs to the building and their faces ton living-picture camera. One of the troupe was "made up" like President Roosevelt, another represented Mr. Booker T. Washington, while others stood for well-known Republican politicians. The pseudo-Roosevelt was repre- sented as raising up, embracing, and finally taking into his carriage the pseudo-Washington, who was represented as disgracefully drunk, while other similar scenes were displayed satirising Mr. Roosevelt's attitude towards the colour problem. The troupe pro- fessed that the whole thing was a joke, but it was more or less evident that the" living pictures," which had of course the Capitol as their background, were intended for use during the forthcoming Presidential election. Fortunately for the credit of America, a detective who was sent after the actors to New York succeeded in obtaining and destroying the negatives of the living, not to say lying, pictures.

div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

Fashion has displayed an unusual and trilly wonderful fidelity to the modes announemd some months ago. and these remain pretty much as they were with but few alterations, and these are so slight as to be only apparent to the initiated. Our skirts are certainly a trifle fuller round the waist than they were, but the fulness is evenly distributed by means of gaugings and tuckings, and the soft folds are so arranged as to still define the outlines of the figure. The perfectly fitting skirt which clings closely to the upper part•of the figure below the waist and flows round the feet in a profusion of frills and flounces is still en evidence, and is adhered to by those whose figures are naturally good and can stand the style, but the portly matron is wise when she declines to make herself ridiculous by adopting such a trying simplicity. There are such charming mus- lins, both spotted and patterned, that one longs for midsummer sunshine in which to disport oneself clad in these dainty diapban-

div.head: PRETTY FROCK.
div.p: A PRETTY FROCK.

ous fabrics. In all the new models the skirt and itr lining are only joined at the waist, and even this junction is not always made, for one underskirt of white or cream silk can do duty for more than one. gown. The upper skirt is generally tastefully gauged or drawn in round the waist, the lower edge being adorned by lace insertions and a lace-trimmed flounce, but simplicity is the feature of these muslin toilettes.

The pretty frock sketched is of white muslin spotted with turquoise blue, the shoulder frills being of muslin embroidered in blue and white, a band of plain white embroidery finishing the neck and wrists, and forming a band down the front of the bodice. Pretty little turquoise blue buttons form the fastenings. The toilette is com- pleted by a blue muslin flop hat trimmed with white lace and embroidery, the flat white crown being of the same blue and white embroidery as the frills. It is a charming dress and hat for a girl of ten to fourteen years. of age.
This is essentially a summer which offers abundant opportunities for economising, for, as most of us know, it is not the outlay incurred in the rpurchasinv of a pretty muslin
A NEAT BLOUSE.
robe with material for the bodice which
makes serious inroads on a moderate dress

allowance but the expense of having it made up by the dressmaker, as the latter often amounts to a larger sum than the cost of the material and trimmings. This year, however, with the shaped skirts all ready for wearing over an underskirt, together with the aid of a good paper pattern for a fashionable blouse shape, such as can be obtained together with simple directions for the cut- ting out and making up of the various parts, any girl should be able to make up pretty costumes herself if she possesses a sewing machine. A neat blouse forms the subject of my second sketch, and is decidedly original as well as smart in design. It could be expressed in the woollen materials if desired, or would look equally charming designed of muslin or silk, with strappings of embroidery or lace, and a pretty tie knotted in front of silk or soft crepe de chine. One can nearly always obtain a little home assistance in fitting on a bodice, and much unnecessary trouble can be avoided by having the pattern cut to measure as is ebligingly done by many firms who make a speciality of this kind of thing, and only charge a few pence more for the extra trouble involved.' Th the skirt
A LACE-TRIMMED HAT.

also is not so difficult an undertaking as it need not be so accurate as a year ago, and should, to be up-to-date, display sundry gaugings immediately below the waist. It will be found a good plan to leave the bodice or blouse unlined, to be woni over a tight- fitting slip of silk or satin. Lace, as we know, is one of the most useful as well as the most fashionable trimmings of the day. It is employed 'everywhere, and perhaps nowhere to such advantage as in the world of millinery. Th.- charming hat depicted is of fine burnt Leghorn straw draped rOund the crown wit folds of tine soft delicately - patterned lace, caught in front by an ornamental buckle. The lace forms a vt-,il at the back, which falls in graceful folds to the shoulders. The edge of the hat i 4 bound with black velvet, and a note of colour is introduced by a cluster of pink roses, which, •although invisible in the sketch, nestle on the hair under the brim at the left side, where it forms an upward curve. For mornieg wear hats of this tone are often only trimmed with black arranged in the form of a smart bow of 'chine silk or as stiff wings- There is some- thingivery chic in this contrast, and it has the Advantage of harmonising with any colour of costume as well as with all sorts of materials. It is, of course, hardly a novelty • as it was with us all last summer.

div.head: FACE TO FACE.
div.p: FACE TO FACE.
BY JOHN W. KNEESHAW, Author of "Norcliffe Court," "The Cost of Hist Vow," "The Cotton Lord's Daughter," &c.

The sun had not long risen above the horizon, and it flooded the great city and the lowlands adjoining, driving away the mists, and even making the pall of smoke look less grey and more fleecy, and giving a touch of crimson to the grey building from which a man had just emerged. The heavy gates had clanged behind him, and for the first time for five years he was a free man, free to go where he would, free to face a world that had no greeting for him. He stood on the white road and looked about him in a dazed, bewilderel sort of way, as if he hardly realised be could go whither he would. He was only a young man yet—not thirty—and, despite the haggard, sullen face, the close-cropped hair, and the defiant mien, he was not unhandsome, for there was an aspect of gentlemanliness about him.

There were a few persons about. watching the prison doors curiously, and a warder stood at the entrance with an air of careless indifference. The man had not expected anyone to meet him, for his term still wanted two years of its close. No one of his former acquaintances knew he was to be set at liberty that day. He had passed out of their world. Yet his heart felt sore that of all he had once known not one was present to welcome him, and there was not one familiar face. It was, he fiercely told himself, but on a piece with the rest. They had forgotten him; he was a pariah, and he cursed the world. _ _ _

Think of it! For five years George Carforth had had the torture of suffering and knowing he was innocent; of bearing in his heart the shame and degradation of guilt, but guiltless ; of knowing that friends were alienated, that he was branded as a criminal, that he was no fit companion for respectable men and women to rub shoulders with, and of knowing it was all undeserved. , And now he was free What s9rt of freedom was it? What had life to offer ? He was without friends, without hope. All that was left was the longing to pay back to the world the injustice he had received.

The knowledge that the strangers were looking at him annoyed him, and he turned impatiently away. A gentleman, kindly disposed, came forward and spoke to him, and received an angry reply. George Carforth wanted no sympathy or pity. What he asked for was justice, and, failing that— revenge. He plunged into the city, anxious to lose himself and to carry out his plans. For five years he had lived for that moment, brooded over it, nurtured his hatred for it, planned against the day of its coming. There whs in his breast more than the pang Of undeserved sufferinc, and reproach. There was the crowning torture of believing that his own friend had done this He knew very little of the world during his five years of incarceration. Happily his parents were dead. They had not lived to see his shame. He had few relatives, and they cared very little about him. He was a disgrace to their honourable lives. Only one, an uncle, his father's brother, had made an effort during the years of imprisonment to see him, and, as the man had spent the brief interview in admonitions to honesty, George Carforth refused to see him or anyone else again. He could not do that now for he was in the world, but his course was mapped out. He was not without money, and he knew that there must be more somewhere, for during the five years the income from his patrimony had been accumulating. His first object was to be avenged on his former bosom friend; his second was to leave the country forever. _ _ _

Five years before he had been a bright young fellow of three-and-twenty, with good prospects. Then had come a charge of forgery, one that he could find no means of disproving. Gradually a chain was wound round him. Circumstantial evidence pointed to him as the guilty person, and the chief witness against him was his bosom friend, Charles Debenharn. A jury of his fellow- countrymen were completely satisfied of his guilt; the judge had expressed approval of their Terdiet, and he was sentenced to seven fears' hard labour. At the time of the trial he had been too think clearly, but the years had provided :wipe time in which to unravel mentally the tangled skein, and it had all come clear. He understood it all now. He had, reviewed the evidence, run over every little incident; and he knew now that Charles Debenham was the forger, and that he had been sacrificed for the sake of, and by, his friend. All the day he lingered about the cigjr. It was not that he was hesitating as to his course. But he had preparations to make and inquiries to set on foot, and he wished to avoid all chance of' recognition. Then, as the evening shadows fell, lie took a ticket for his native town. There he was compelled to meet those he had known. He shrank at first from the ordeal, but assuming a callousness he did not feel, and rudeness foreign to his nature, he faced old acquaintances, and produced on their minds a worse impression than ever. One or two attempted good advice, but no man gave it twice... _

The afternoon of the next day found him outside the home of his one-time friend. He had traced him to a villa on the outskirts of a little town. The house stood a hundred yards from any other. It was a peaceful, pleasant little place. There was a green lawn in front surrounded by trees and shrubs, and the road ran past it. There was plenty and comfort written large all over the place. The lot of Charles Debenham had evidently fallen in pleasant places, and George Carforth mentally contrasted his old friend's posi- tion with his own, and hatred • grew deeper in his heart. It was hard to feel that he had just come from a prison with a tickst-of-leave in his pocket, while the guilty man should be finding life so pleasant. It was his duty to see to a more equitable distribution of suffering. There was a little copse on one si 'e of the lawn, and by passing into the adjoining field be contrived to obtain the shelter of the trees, where he could watch the house and remain him- self unseen. He wanted to make observations to see how best his revenge could be carried. out. He - had not been there half-an-hour when he saw that which added to his longing for vengeance. It was a beautiful autumn day, and the front door was standing wide open. Presently there came out on tie Awn two persons, a woman leading a little girl of about three years of age. He gasped in agony. Why had he never thought of this? Why had no one told him that Charles Debenham had done him worse wrong than swear his liberty away? He knew his old friend was a villain, but it had never occurred,t ie him that Charles Debenhaiu would take adva,:age of the seven years' imprisonment to win the girl plighted to himself, or that she ‘c-ti!d give herself to the man who had betrayed her lover. Five .years before he had been filled with radiant happiness, because Clara Dayton had confessed her love to him. When the arrest came he had been full of dreams for the future. When be was led away a convict, more than half the agony had been caused by the knowledge that be had lost the one woman he loved. He realised that she could not marry a convict, and if she were willing to wait and throw in her lot with him, her friends would not nermit the sacrifice. But the 1 ain of the knowledge that he had lest her was as nothing to the torture of knowing Charles Debenham had!won her. Yet here she was, the wife of his old comrade, the mistress of his horse, the mother of his child. Oh! the agony of it! In his fury and torture he pressed his face into the soft grass to stifle a groan which was half a curse, and clenched the ground with his hands. _ _

When he looked up again Clara had seated herself under a tree on the other side of the lawn and had taken the child on her knee, and the two etere chatting merrily, laughing heartily, and punctuating their pleasant discourse with kisses and endearments. Clara looked le,s radiant. than when he last saw her, but the gentle smile that hovered round her lips as she talked with the little one was very sweet, and recalled that happy day when he had first held her in his arms. Then there was the sound of wheels on the road, the garden gate flew open, and the child suddenly scrambled to the ground and rushed off to meet a gentleman who was .entering, It. wns Charles DebenhAm himself, and, picking tile tiny dot up in his arms and kissing her, he crossed to Clara's side, she on her part receiving him with .a ..glad smile that was gall and wormwood to the unseen watcher. - _

It was too far away for Gearge •Carforth to hear -What was said. 'There was an earnest conversation 'for some moments, then. Clara rose hurriedly, and 'they all passed into the howl. A. quarter of an hour later they emerged once more, and this time Clara was dressed for a journey.
She was assisted into a gig, Charles sprang In after her, and they drove down the road, leaving the little one peeping out through the gate after

WArri. • - hen they had finally disappeared the child returned contentedly to the lawn, and began to play happily. Meantime the thought of a terrible revenge had come to the watcher. Vengeance was here to his hand—a more sure and safe retaliation than he had thought of before. Half-an-hour later there was no child playing on the lawn, and when a nurse, whose business it was to keep an eye on its doings, looked out, it was -nowhere to be seen. It had vanished completely. But what the servant did not see, because of the intervening grove of shrubs, was a man nearly a mile away, hurrying over the fields with a little girl in his arms. George Carforth had no difficulty in obtaining posse'ssion of the child. It wandered to his side of the lawn. Then a man's face rose over a bush and a pair of arms was stretched towards it. He was a little taken aback when in the utmost confi- dence and readiness the little dot, after one glance _ _ _ .

at his face, came forward and iielded herself to him. The spirit of trust and possibly of adventure was great in its tiny soul. There was not a.person in sight, and, picking up the baby, he plunged into the copse and out into the sunlit fields beyond. He had not had much experience with children, and he expected this one to cry lustily, and he would have acted sharply if occasion required. Instead the small maiden shewed not the least fear or alarm, but seemed thoroughly to enter into the adventure. "Going to papa ? " she asked, looking smilingly into his eyes with her little hand on his neck. "Yes," he answered, and she clapped her hands merrily. _ _ _

Apparently she considered it a very happy arrangement for her to be carried rapidly over the fields where there were so many novel things to be seen; and George Carforth, to his own astonish- ment, found himself pointing out the cows, and sheep, and other objves of interest, even while he wcs intent on hurrying on and avoiding all observation. "What is oo name ?" she asked. •
"George," he replied. "Doge!" she repeated. "I likes ro, Doge," and to his dismay two tiny arms were placed round his neck and two ripe little lips were held up to be kissed.

Of course he kissed her. He would have been all brute had he refused a child's innocent kiss. He was less brute after he had kissed her. It was the first kiss he had known for years, and part of his morose bitterness disappeared with it. His revenge was not going to be so easy. Had the child struggled or cried he could have used it roughly. He had intended to rush with it to London, and there lose it in the slums, to grow up as it might. It was a diabolical revenge, worthy of a fiend. George Carforth was not quite fiend, though well advanced, so he felt a little compunc- tion in the face of the child's confidence. For the next half-hour the baby was puzzled, and it had its doubts concerning its new acquaint- ance, for George would not speak to it. He was gloomy and morose, and a scowl rested on his face. To tell the truth, he had repented him of his kind- ness to the child, and he was recounting to himself the wrongs he had suffered at the hands of the baby's parents, and he was trying to steel his heart against its blandishments and against the gentler thoughts that had begun to spring up in his heart. At last lie reached a place where he could rest for an hour or two secure from observation. It was a little dingle among the woods, and here he decided to stay until it was dark. Then he would take the child's hat and lay it on the banks of the river near its home. After that he would make his way to a quiet railway station, and plunge into London while the distracted parents were examin- ing the river in the belief that their, darling had perished in its waters. It would be a glorious revenge for all he had suffered. He sat down, on the grass and placed the cbild beside him. - -
"What is your name, little one?" he asked it, and there was a tenderness in his voice which surprised himself. "Dolly," was the reply. "Come and play with the Vowers."

There was an air of imperious command about the words and the tone which amused him, and he laughed. It was his first laugh -for years, and he felt better for it. The laugh seemed to amuse llf, and she joined in with a shrill shout of laughter. The prison authorities would have been amazed could they have seen Convict 215 during the next hour. He had always been well behaved but' sullen, and yet within thirty-six hours of his leaving prison he was playing with a little child, laughing quietly at her remarks, trotting over the grass by her side, plucking wild flowers for her, tying wreaths of blossoms round her golden head, and she was as happy as if no harm hung over her bonny sweet form. At last she was tired, and he sat down on a bank and she crept into his arms. "Doge," she said, "when is we going to papa ? " "Presently," he replied. "Does Dolly want to go?" "Yes. Where is he?" •

_ - "Gone away with mamma." • "Dolly's tired. Let us go home to mamma." That was not, however, in George's programme, so he began to weave a story for the child's amuse- ment, and before long the sleepy eyes closed and Dolly was fast asleep. The light in the west had already began to fade, and he conceived that the time had come to begin the next part of his intentions. He laid her gently down on the grass, and taking off his co'at placed it over her. Then taking her sun-bonnet he left her sleeping, and began to retrace his steps to the river. It was not a very large stream, and he calculated that by the time he could go, deposit the hat and _return, it would be dark enough for him to start for the station en route for London, and there was still enough of bitter malice in his heart for him to gloat over the pain of Charles Dehenham and his wife at. their loss. Part of his programme he carried out. A part broke down. he task of carrying the hat and depositing it on the river's brink was not as •easy as it, 1-oked, for a couple of men were about, and as he did not wish to be seen he was delayed. The result was that by the time he returned to the dingle where he had left Dolly it was rawly dark. A great horror fell on him when he reached the spot. The child was no longer'there ! The coat uneer wh'ch he Fad left her lying was there, hot the child i ad vani,hed. In a flash he saw what had linppened. Dolly had awoke, and finding herself alone she had wandered away into the woods, protably terrified at the dark- ness and loneliness. Heaven help himl She would wander nbout all night, and in the morning would be found lying dead from fright and exposure. And he II o'dd be guilty of her death! •In a moment a great love for the little one rushed info his I eart. She had been so fair to

look upon, so loving, so trustful, so innocent. She had been the only creature who for five long years shad shewn him love and confidence. Her innocent childish kis; was still warm on his lips. Even while he had plotted against her, she had nestled into his Aries confidingly. And she had wandered away to die! lie could no bear the thought of her suffering. his vengeance was forgotten, swallowed up in remorse ard anguish. He reviled himself to think that all t hat his plans of revenge had accom- plished was the suitering and pain of a tender, loving little child. "Doily, Dolly," he called, but the wind moving the trees was all the answer he got. Then he began to dash to and fro, frantically calling her min's, pPering 'among the bushes for a glimpse of white dress. But it was all in vain, 'Said when tho darkness had settled down he was still in the dingle alone. For an hour after it was quite dark he continued his „arch, but it was with despair in his heart. One project now took possession, of him. He could not callously turn away and leave the child to perish, • even though it was what he had, actually intended and planned. The only course left was to go to the child's home, tell his story, and obtain help to loos for her. He shrank from siich a course. To go back to Charles Debenham as a suppliant for pardon was too much. He could not do it But finally his , manhood co.nTiered. The evil spirit in him succinnbed to his. better nature, and he turned resolutely. He had not gone a hundred yards before a child's faint cry reached his far. Swift as an arrow he turned in the direction and' sped *way. And under a hedge he found the little ones crying quietly. "Doge, take me home? I's tired," the baby vote, said, piteously, as he picked her up and pressed her to his heart. "I will, Dolly darling," he said, and folding her in his arms he started off again. There Were lights in the house of Charles Dobenham when he drew near. He understood. Search had been made for the lost one. In all probability search was still being made, and the household had not retired. By this time Dolly was asleep again. A French

window was open, and hp stepped into the room where a gas-jet, turned very low, gave a dim light. He was in a room cosily and almost luxuriously furnished. He laid the sleeping baby on A soft couch, and hastily threw over her a soft wrap ne caught up from a chair. Then his lips lightly touched its forehead, and he turned to O. But a Taney took him to see if possible now Charles Debenham felt at his loss. He had made restitution, but he had not foregone his revenge. He was inside his enemy's house, why should be notkearn more?

He opened the door of the room stealthily and found he was in a dimly-lit passage. 'Nearly Opposite was another door partly open; with a strong light pouring out of the aperture. He peeped in. Debenham was seated in front, of a desk with a child's hat before him, his head bowed on his hands. He was alone. Carforth, on a sudden impulse, pushed the door open and stepped into the room, closing the door behind him. A key was in the lock and he turned it. The noise caused the occupant to look up quickly, and his eyfs met those of the convict. "You, Carforth!" he exclaimed. "I thought perhaps you would come. I heard this morning that you were at liberty. lam sorry I cannot feel enthusiastic, for I suffer a terrible loss." He rose and held out his hand. "I can guess I am not very welcome. I never supposed I should be," said Carforth with a sneer. "You are a coward and a thief!" Debenham recoiled.

"What do-you mean ?" he asked: "You know what I mean, you traitor! I did not coma as a friend; I came ail an enemy. I came with murder in my heart! Do you think five years of gaol makes angels? Sit down, and if you call out or try to summon assistance you die " and he held a revolver levelled at Debenham.
The latter sat down calmly aftli-ough he was deadly pale. "Don't be a fool, George!" he said. "What do you want?"

- "I want to tell you I mow your villainy. For five years I have brooded over it. You know lam innocent ? " "1 do." "And yet you swore my liberty away to save yourself !" "You are under some delusion. I swore to nothing but what was true." "You knew I was innocent, but you never spoke because you were the guilty party. You forged the cheque." - "That is not true.

"It is true. Do you think I do not know, that I cannot see and understand ? You have lived in comfort; what hat my life been?" "I am vcry sorry, George---" "Are you? Then do the right thing. You see this paper. It is a confession of your guilt. You will sign it now or you die." Debenhani took the paper and glanced it through. "You don't expect me to sign this ?" he said. "I did not forge the cheque." "You sign or die! You knew J. was innocent." "I know now. I.have known a few hours, that is all."
"You lie! You have known all along." "I have known since the forger confessed to-day. Cease this fooling, George. I am in too deep trouble to jest."

"Aye!" laughed Carforth. "You know part of my five years' anguish to-day. How do you like it.? But your pain will be short, my disoTace is lifelong." Just then there was a child's cry outside, and rushing feet were heard in the passage. "Charles! Charles!" called a voice Carforth knew. "Dolly is here quite safe. She was asleep on a sofa in the drawing-room." Debenham rose excitedly, but his visitor covered him with the weapon.

"I have not done yet," he said, in a hoarse whisper. "Answer that you will be at liberty presently." Debenham called out as he was bidden, and the steps went along the passage, though Clara was evidently puzzled by his conduct, "Now attend to me," said Carforth. " "What do you want ? " "That. paper signing. Then I leave you." "I will not sign a lie." "Then I shall shoot you! I am determined to have either restitution or revenge. You stole my good name. You have also stolen the girl I was engazed to." "You mean Clara Dayton?" "Yes ; your wile." There was a smile round Debenham's lips for a moment.

"You are mistaken in supposing I was the forger," he said, gravely. "Listen and I will tell you the true story. When you were convicted two persons believed you innocent. I was one, Clara Dayton the other. We have never relinquished that faith, but we have tried to prove your innocence. We set to work to trace the thief. Clara's intuition soon put her on the right track; but only to-day—the day after your release—have we accomplished our task. In my presence and that of Clara the criminal confessed his guilt."
"Who was he ? " "David Wilkinson." "Good Heavens! And I thought it was you V

"He is dead. lie died. soon after his con- fession. To-morrow full proof of your innocence will te in the hands of the Home Secretary." Carforth sank into a chair. "Good Heavens!" he exclaimed. "And it was I who stole your child in revenge!" "I guessed as much. But you brought her back." "Can you forgive me ? "I do, and I congratulate you on your innocence being made manifest." Then Carforth gave way. The weight of five years was lifted. He had entered the sunlight. He laid his head on his hands and sobbed like a child. Presently be rose. "I shall want to know more by-and-bye, but it is enough. I know how touch I owe you. I have wronged you. Let ma go." "No ; you must stay." "I can't do that. I shall never be able to look at you again after I have wronged you so cruelly. I dare not meet your wife. She will hoe° me. I loved her once. You are better than I and deserve her, but let me go." "You cannot go now. You must stay till day- light. Remain in this room, and if you want to go in the morning I will not 'object." And at last Carforth agreed to stay in that room till the morning. Debenham drew a chair in front of the fire, and leaving his guest there he slipped away to see his recovered treasure. For some minutes Carforth sat looking into the fire. He was overwhelmed at the turn events had taken, and full of remorse at his own mistakes. The very place where he had plotted murder seemed to choke him. He could not stay. He must go. • He started to his feet as the door opened, and he was face to face with his old love. She was still young and beautiful. She gave no start of surprise, and it was clear she had come knowing he was there. He had expected loathing from her at his abduction Of the child. But there was in her eyes pity and love instead. "George!" she said, softly. . "Mrs. Debenham," he said, with an effort, "I beg your forgiveness." "Yon needn't. I have nothing to forgive. George. I have felt for you. I have suffered with you these years." "But you married another." "Look," she said, and she held out her left hand. There was no wedding-ring on it. Instead there was a circlet which he well remembered—the diamond ring he himself had put on her fitSer nearly six years before when they two had plighted their troth.. "What does it mean ? " he gasped. made another mistake ?"
" HaTe I

-- "Yes, dear. Charles married my sister Agnes. I—have—wait ed---and-hoped—and—i—still wear your ring l" Then he stepped forward and took her in his arms, and the five years of misery slipped entirely from his shoulders.
Min END. 1 A. CHILD'S DEATH AT WIDNES.

Mr. Samuel Brighouse—, -c'oroner held an inquest at the Police Station, Widnes, on Tuesday afternoon, on the body of Agnes Jordan, the six • months old daughter of Jo'hii and Mary Anne Jordan, Nelson-street, Widnes.-- John Jordan, bricklayer, said his daughter had been • unwell for some weeks. On Saturday week witness went home and gave, his wife the whole of his wages, afterwards remonstratinz with her for running him into debt. At half-past three he went te sleep en the sofa, and when he awoke some time after he found his wife had left home, and up to the present had not been able to trace her.- -Dr. Hutchinson said he had attended the child from time to time.. She was in a delicate state of health. ,'After death, on the 21st inst., he made a post-mortem examination. No marks were found externally. Th, body was much emaciated, <lnd sceighed about that of a new) y-born child. The internal organs were healthy, with the exception of the lungs, which were in a very advanced stage of inflammation.. The cause of death was inflammation of the lungs, but he could not commit I himself as to the cause, whether of neglect or natural 1 causes.—A verdict in accordance with the medical ! evidence was returned.

div.head: ITALY IN LONDON.
div.p: ITALY IN LONDON.

Each year the directors of Earl's Court, •-ondon's most welcome purveyors of summer amusement, go one better than the year be- fore, and this season they have again ex.celled 'themselves with the Italian Exhibition. -Prom the unspeakable atmosphere of the Underground the jaded Londoner steps out -in a moment into Southern splendour, and the realism is almost bewildering in its effect •at first. There are many striking and won- derful features, but unquestionably the most Popular is "Venice by Night." Mr. Herman Hart, the architect and artist, has worked wonders, and reproduced the Queen of the Adriatic with marvellous accuracy and effect. Here by the light of innumerable lamps and the aid of gondoliers, who have under their •Charge a fleet of cthirty-six genuine gondolas, the Londoner can travel the canals and see the sights of Venice in miniature. There is the Doge's Palace, the Campanile (now a ruin in real Venice), the Palace Darla, the Churches of St. Mark and St. Maria, and the Bridge of Sighs, the Rialto Bridges, and the Three Arches. There is three-quarters of a mile of .eanal, and Italian love songs float across the :lagoon. The other sights are legion. There IS the famous Blue Grotto of Capri, wonder- fully reproduced; tableaux of the Roman Porum ; representation of an Arctic icefield, as seen from the deck of the Duke of Abruzzi's " Stella Polare," with ingenious lighting effects which reproduce the Aurora Borealis; a fine collection of pictures; "La Scala," the Italian theatre; and a thousand - and - one Other things to fill up a long day. Round he Wheel has sprung up au old Italian town in keeping with the rest of the Exhibition. The Great Wheel is still going, as is that old favourite, the switchback, and there are always bans playing for the promenaders. One notabre new -feature of this year's Exhi- bition is Sir Hiram Maxim's fixed flying Machine, which is hugely popular as a new sensation, and every visitor for a modest fee can have his first taste of the locomotion of t. he future, and glean a little practical insight Into aerostatics. Altogether, Earl's Court Ilas surpassed itself, and it is certainly the :gaYest and pleasantest corner in London 011 -a warm night.

div.head: KING'S VISIT TO KIEL.
div.p: KING'S VISIT TO KIEL.

The greatest interest has been aroused by the announcement of the King's intention to visit the Kaiser at Kiel Regatta, which takes Place during the last week of next month. Ying Edward had intended to go to Potsdam Jast month to pay the Emperor William a State visit, but the health of the latter necessitated a voyage to the Meditteranean and the Icing's plans had to be altered on this account. It is an open secret that nothing could have been more appropriate or have given the Kaiser greater pleasure than the proposed visit to Kiel, which is one of his hobbies. Already upwards of six hundred entries have been sent in, and it is expected That now many more will arrive before the first of June out of compliment to the royal reunion. In addition, the Kaiser has ordered the whole available German Fleet to be -mobilised to welcome King Edward with full --111°110nrs. The King will cross on the Victoria and Albert, and will no doubt be escorted

tY a British fleet to return the compliment. ;Lints Kiel will witness a great meeting of ''-wo kings in state, and the sight should be 'a very impressive one. Already the hotel tiotel accommodation has all been booked up, ut the Kaiser, with his usual promptness in °vercoming difficulties, has arranged with lierr Bailin, of the Hamburg-American line, :I.° bring round to Kiel one of his great Iners, the Graf I,Valdersee, and use it as a 40,at* in- hotel, thereby making up for the 1I 'll.niency on land. How far the meeting of lag and Kaiser will have a political • aspect 3 at present doubtful, but it is significant and sure to do good by promoting a better 7tate of things between, Germany and our- elves after a period of strained relations. threadyl there are signs in the German press at an improvement in our international relations would be welcomed. But it is ';a•rlY days yet to speak more definitely than express a certainty that this will be the •e. whether anything more solid. should .esult or not.

div.p: SKETCHES AT EARL'S COURT.
MR. A. W. BLACK

the Unionists into conflicting units. The first phase was that the Chamberlainites or Preferential Tariff members—a very large consideration in a division—were put into such a position by the phrasing of the motion that they saw no option but to abstain from voting. To avoid this contre- temps, Mr. Chamberlain himself ' put an amendment on the paper, which cleared all obstacles out of their way and seemed for the time to relieve the tension. But on the day before the debate the Unionist Free Fooders held a meeting and decided that they must vote against Mr. Chamberlain's amendment, which meant a matter of ninety

votes at least on a division. So the Premier after a hurried consultation with his col- leagues himself handed in an amendment the very last thing on Tuesday night, which, of course, in deference to his official !position, took precedence of Mr. Chamberlain's. Wed- nesday's debate was full of interest and once more Mr. Balfour showed his skill as a Parliamentary leader in taking his supporters into the lobby. The result was that, with absentions and adverse votes on the part of some of the Unionists, Mr. Black's motion was rejected •by a majority of 5;, and the 6ituation was saved. The affair from an outside point of view was interesting as an example of Parliamentary tactics and the way the game of politics is played.
THE WORLD'S RICHEST MAN. ilfrAe

It has often been discussed and argued as to who is the world's richest man, and, apropos of this, a Wall Street banker has just issued a very interesting pamphlet, in which he unhesitatingly gives the palm to Mr. John Rockefeller, the president of the Standard 0 ii Trust. He assesses him as •the, world's only billionaire, and ,places his for- tune at ii,000,00 0,0 o dollars, or £200,00 0 , 000 is terl ing ! No one else is likely to come into competition with such vast wealth, beside which even the MR. ROCKEFELLER. millions of Mr. Carnegie and the Vanderbilts sink into comparative insig- nificance. Mr. Rockefeller's holding represents half the wealth of the mighty •and auto- cratic Standard Oil Trust, which is assessed at £4.00,000,000, or two billion dollars; and of the remaining moiety, Mr. William Rockefeller has the comfortable little slice of £40,000,000. Still there is room in the concern for several other vast fortunes, which are owned by Messrs. Rogers, Flayler, Arch- bold, and others. He takes no part in public Life or politics, but he has his representatives and nominees everywhere. Of all his vast wealth, all he spends on himself is a few hundred a year. .He is a dyspeptic and fervently religious, and his only hobbies are golf and yachting. The result is that each year's accumulation of income is in itself an immense fortune.

div.head: JAPANESE NAVAL DISASTER.
div.p: JAPANESE NAVAL DISASTER.

The terrible calamity which has just befallen the Japanese navy by the loss of the battleship Hatsuse and the cruiser Yoshino will evoke the deepest sympathy from all classes in England. The battleship, it is stated, struck a Russian mine, whilst the cruiser was rammed by a sister vessel in a dense fog. The loss of life is over seven hundred, only 390 of the two crews which numbered i, Too being saved. From accounts to hand it appears whilst Admiral Togo was covering landing operations Admiral Dewa was watching Port Arthur, and in one of the fogs so prevalent in the Yellow _ Sea at this time of the year the cruiser Kasuga, one of the new boats recently sent out from Genoa, rammed and sank the Yushino. The disaster to the Hatsuse happened about ten miles from P' here she struck

div.head: BATTLESHIP HATSUSE.
div.p: THE BATTLESHIP HATSUSE.

a mine. Help was quickly forthcoming, but oilt of a crew of 740 only 300 were saved. This was probably due to the absence of sufficient boats to carry so many .men. Whilst the Russians claim to have laid the mines, and the Japanese Admiral himself says that, the catastrophe was due to a Russian mine, it appears from the statement of a correspon- dent that many mines are adrift. The Hatsuse was one of Japan's best battleships in regard to size, equipment and speed. She was of 13.,000 tons displacement, ,and was built at the Elswi,ck works in 1899. She carried 741 men and was commanded by. tCaptain Y Nakao. The Yoshino was an un- armoured cruiser of 4,180 tons, commanded by Captain G. Saiki, and was built by Armstrong, Whitworth and Co., at Elswick, 1892. She carried a crew of 300.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

EARLESTPOVN MAY QUEEN. Attention is called in our advertising 'cola nag to the Earlestown May Queen festivities which are being held this afternoon on the Elrlestown market ground. The proceeds, as in previous years, are to be- devoted to St. John's Church completion fund, and given tine weather the festivities promise to be a big success. A procession will be formed at two o'clock and parade through the principal streets in the town headed by the Warrington Legh-street brass band. Several bands will take part, and numerous characters will be represented, for whick prizes will be given. Miss Martha Adams is this year's May Queen. A strong committee has been hard at work making the necessary arrangements, the Rev. T. R. Matthews being chairman, Messrs. Molyneux and Pimblett treasurers, and Mr. S. Kilmister secretary, by whom all particulars will be given. Convenient trains will he run from towns in the immOiate vicinity.

gressive candidate in Mr. Thomas Richards, miners secretary. It is a pity that similarly cordial relations between the two " for- ward " parties are not more widespread. .In Warrington, for instance, a better understanding would be welcomed in many quarters. It might be understood that, should the Liberals fail to carry the seat at the next general election, the Labour men should be given the opportunity of trying their strength. In the meantime, as we have maid over and over agiin, it is to the interest of the Labour party in Warrington to support Mr. A. H. Crosfield who has spoken in certain and reassuring tones on the questions closely concern- ing trade unionists and Labour men. He is not merely a Liberal but, above all, a Progressive and as such he shoukl command the support of every man who desires enlightened legislation and no slavery beneath the British flag.

The three Warrington trading firms who peti- tioned against the Manchester Ship Canal Bill have every reason to congratulate themselves upon the protective clauses they have obtained from the company. The clauses are set forth in another column and they bear evidence of a disposi- tion on the part of the Manchester Ship Canal Company to meet the grievance of the traders in a fair and liberal spirit. If the company carry out their obligations in the same way, we shalt have reached the end of the vexatious and costly litigation between the town and the Ship Canal Company. Messrs. Fairclough's water rights have been bought out entirely, and in fn- tura the engines at the Mersey mills will be driven by steam power instead of water no wer. Messrs. Monks, Hallaand Company and Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons have also secured recognition of their valuable rights on the river, and clauses have been obtained securing the pay— ment of compensation for loss or injury which may be sustained by any interference with them. Altogether the interests of tha town and its indos- tries have been guarded, and the effect on trade cannot fail to be beneficial in the long run.

There was none of the bitterness attendant upon defeat shown at the annual meeting of the Warrington Football Club on Tuesday evening. The members have apparently recovered their mental balance in the four weeks that have elapsed since the fiasco at Weaste, when Warrington suc- cumbed ingloriously in the final for the Northern Union Cup. All was peace and quietness at the annual meeting, the reports were adopted without criticism, the committee and officers were specially thanked for their services, and re-elected en blue. The members have reason to be well satisfied with the working of the Club, for there is once more a balance on the right side after a very expensive season. Something like L'4,000 has been handled by the Club during the past eight months, figures which speak eloquently of the growth of the game in the district. A player now- a-days can make quite a little for- tune from his participation is first-class football and we are glad to know that some of the men who do duty for Warrington have the common sense to recognise the importance of thrift. The Club supporters—and their name is legion—will be glad to learn that there is no probability of the Club being disturbed at Wilderspool for many years to come. A goad ground could easily be , got elsewhere but there is every desire to retain the present excellent headquarters. May we add here, a note of sympathy with the family of the late Mr. W. Dillon, a highly-respected old playing member and ex-official, whose death occurred suddenly last week-end.

There was" much ado about nothing" at the Police Court yesterday when the Education Com- mittee summoned Mr. W. A. Proud for not sending his daughter to school. Tne facts of the case were that the child was delicate and Mr. Proud had a medical certificate as to her unfitness for school, but in the course of several calls the Inspector had been unable to see the certificate, because it was in Mr. Proud's possession and he was out. There- fore the; Education authorities summoned Mr. Proud, only to withdraw the case on the produc- tion of the certificate. It is easy to find fault with both sides. Mr. Proud might have sent his certifi- cate and the educition authorities might have been less arbitrary. Tuey knew the child was unfit for school, aud if they had been discreet they would have kept out of court with such a flimsy case. There is plenty of scope for their endeavours in seeing that children who are fit and well attend school regularly, without worrying people like Mr. Proud in a spirit of pettishness, and wasting rate- payers' money in useless prosecutions.

A list of firms has been quoted by the Tariff Reform Commission as having given evidence be- fore it respecting the iron and steel trade. All the firms mentioned are producers of raw material, or partly manufactured material, which is used by manufacturers in making finished goods. Where one man is employed in making this rough material hundreds are employed in carrying the material to its various stages of completion in the form of the finished product. It is not denied that these trades feel the effect of the importation of cheap foreign iron and steel; but would it be advisable to shut up the thousands of factories • throughout the kingdom which can only meet the foreign competition in finished goods by purchasing their material at some lo to 20 per cent, cheaper from countries which are not so handicapped (ts we are by mining royalties and crushing railway rates ?

There is a typical case which shows how the matter works out in its practical aspect. A large i firm of manufacturers n London uses 109 tons monthly of a certain material which they buy from Germany at £7 los. per ton, but for which they would have to pay £9 103. per ton in England, the carriage alone being 17s. Oct. per ton. Now this firm has a large export trade, and, as it is, can only just hold its own; but where would this trade ue if they had to pay nearly 22 a ton more for their material in order to compensate a few producers for their commercial and political disabilities? It is certain their export trade would be gone, and their home trade would be considerably lessened, on account oi the necessarily advanced prices on all their goods. Look at the Protectionist scheme as we may, it amounts to this—sacrificing the many for the few, and the c9ntralisation of capital instead of its distribution.

The leather goods' exports of Germany are among the many industries of the Fatherland which are in anything but a prosperous con- dition. In the current issue of the Free Trader" it is shewn by the official figures that the expott of coarse leather wares (saddlery, trunks, harness, heavy boots, &;c.) has been slowly falling since 1889, when it amounted to £340,000, to £298,000 in 1902. Fine leather goods, consisting of boots and shoes, Morocco and Levant wares, shew evsn a more startling decline. Thus, from a value of £3,850,000 in 1889 they have fallen to £1,407,000 in 1902. As show- ing Germany's inability to cultivate an export trade in better class boots and shoes, it is worthy of note that her importation of these goods is 25 per cent. greater than the export. One reason is the duty on tanning materials, and the other the ability of Austrian manufacturers to compete aith their German rivals owing to the absence of any duty on imported leather.

I Americans often marvel—in American publica- tions—that the literature of their country receives so little recognition from Europe. American stories are read in England, some of Clem, too, on the Continent; but American literature, as such, is not recognised, nor, indeed, is it known. Mrs. Gertrude Atherton, who, as a great-grand-niece of Benjamin Franklin and a writer of some dis- tinction, has some claim to be heard, discusses in the "North American Review" the question, "Why is American Literature Bourgeois ? " Americanism—apart from literature—she regards as a new genius. It is like nothing else in the world, with its vast creative energy, its contempt of convention, its disregard of the limits which ordinary people place upon personal capacity. The American woman carries all before her in Europe, because she has an originality which the more cultivated European woman does not possess. Why, then, asks 11irs. Atherton, does not this nation,

Half the troubles of THE NEED OF RU'SSIA.. Russia ha this war are due to dissen- sions among the CZAR'S advisers, if such a term can be applied to the officials who quarrel with one another with so little regard for the interescs of their count'ry. Admiral ALRXEIEFF, who has done nothing of any value since the war began, seems to be again seeking distinction by thwarting his colleagues. He is said to have vetoed a plan of Admiral SKRYDLOFF'S for gaining access to Port Arthur, and to have dma las best to prevent that officer from reaching Vladi- vostock. If General KUROPA.TKIN ware able to concentrate his mind upon resistance to the Japanese advance in Manchuria, he would have ample occupation. But, in addition to this, he has to squabble with Admiral ALEXEIEFF. All this points to a disorganisation which shews that the Russian bureaucratic system is no more adapted to the necessities of war than it is to the arts of peace. It has been said, not without reason, that a democratic system of government sliews to greater advantage in peace than in war time. Military historians find proof of this in the Civil War in America, which, they say, would have been appreciably shortened if the civilian authorities on both sides had abstained from interference with military strategy. LINCOLN, who knew nothing about war, disturbed the plans of his commanders until he saw the expediency of giving absolute control of the Northern armies to General GRANT. LEE was prevented by timid counsels at Richmond from marching on WASHINGTON after his victory at Ball Ran. But it is not the politicians in Russia who mar the calculations of the soldiers in the field. Itis the universal official habit, military and civil, of subordinating the public interests to the private advantage or personal pique of the individ- ual soldier or statesman.

The CZAR is an autocrat only in name. Whether NICHOLAS 11. will have the firmness to recall Admiral ALEXEIEFF remains to be seen; but it is plain that a real autocrat would have done this two months ago. He would not have appointed General KUROPATKIN to the military command in Manchuria and left that of-112er to fight A.LEXEIEFF as wail as tha itivatier. It was gravely announced in R issia the othir day that although Kuropatkin was supposed to command in Manchuria he had no authority over Linovitch, who corn:nands at Viadivostock ! The Japanese may conduct the attack upon a strategic plan which subordinates every movement to one great purpose. But while Karopatkin in Man- churia is quarrelling with ALEXEIEFF over the plan of defence, the commander at Vladivostock is to be left to the inspiration of unshackled genius. Perhaps he is by no means enthusiastic over the arrival of Admiral SKRYDLOFF ; and we may hear before long that the military and naval experts at Vladivostock are repeating the comedy of bickerings at Mukden. We are not] told very much about the views of G-meral STOESSEL at Port Arthur; but he may be relieved by the turn of events which has spared him the pleasure of Admiral SKRYDLOFF'S society. The Ruasian Army it appears,does not love the Russian Navy. When the French cynic said that the misfortunes of our I best friends are secretly pleasing to us he did not know the relations between the "sister services" in Russia. The recent mbfortunes of the Navy are openly gratifying to the military officials, who seem unable to regard them as mis- fortunes to their country. This lack of solidarity in the Russian system of government has moved a friendly observer to remark that " the conduct of modern war renders indispensable a minimum of modern institutions, which will guarantee the ful- filment of agreements with contractors and the execution of orders given to the personnel of the Administration." Moreover, "there must be effective surveillance of officials, and that can only be secured by the grant of a certain amount of liberty to the Press." But where are the will and the capacity to execute reforms which would mean nothing short of a revolution?

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Police Station last evening on the body of Eveline Warburton, aged 3 years, daughter of William Warburton, wiredrawer, 121, Wellfield-street, who was drowned in the St. Helens and Sankey Canal on Thursday. —Beatrice Northorn (14), of Lloyd-street, a nurse girl employed by Mr. and Mrs. Warburton, stated that on the morning in question she took deceased and another child for a.walk. She had passed over Buttermilk (canal) Bridge, when she m:ssed deceased and on looking round saw her in the middle of the canal. Thomas Knox, of Mill-lane, recovered the body.—ln answer to the Coroner, Detective Barlow said it was practically impossible for a child to fall over the bridge itself into the canal but the ends'of the bridge were unprotected—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death and ex- pressed sympathy with the parents. Deceased's father said he did not in any way complain of the nurse girl's conduct.

div.head: Wild Flowers at the Museum.
div.p: Wild Flowers at the Museum.

_ There is at present on view on the west staircase of the Museum, an interesting collection of wild flowers gathered from the country side around Warrington. To children especially, the collection should prove interesting and instructive. The flowers are grouped according to the family of plants to which they belong and the common name of each flower is given as well as the scientific name. Nature studies of this kind cannot fail to give additional interest to the country walks of children by enabling them to distinguish the various kinds of: wild flowers Which meet the eye at every turn. In order to encourage the collection of wild flowers the Curator will be pleased to receive flowers for exhibition. Amongst those on view at the present time are the bluebell, marsh-marigold, red campion, the holly (in flower), hawthorn, wood sorrel may flower, sage, dead nettle, apple blossom, common arum, and many other varieties. The collection also includes specimens of abnormal growths in plants, illustrating the pernicious effect:of gall and fungi attacks. A section of a black currant bush is shown, which has become barren owing to an attack of an insect known as the mite gall. In the botany section of the museum on the top storey, models of flowers are shown with the different parts labelled and fully described.

A fire broke out in a large shed containing hay and straw on the farm of Mr, John Bridge, GlazebroA last Friday evening. The fire brigade were immedi- ately summoned to the scene, and after playing on the shed for about two hours succeeded in extinguishing the flames. The shed was completely gutted, a Per" tion of the corrugated iron roof being melted. Tho damage is estimated at £5OO, and is covered bi insurance. It is believed that the shed was ac,cident- ally fired by a small boy.

Cross-examined by 'Mr. Gill: Major Wilkinson apologised to him first thing next morning. As far as witness was concerned, that closed the incident. OTHER EVIDENCE. Captain Harold A. Denham, of the King's Liverpool Regiment, was also of the opinion that Major Wilkin- son was drunk. He first noticed the change in his manner when the Major was called upon to make the farewell speech. Four bottles of champagne were drunk at the dinner. He believed Major Wilkinson had nothing but champagne. Lieutenant E. C. Fane, who also dined at the mess, thought Major Wilkinson was the worse for drink. This closed the prosecution and the Court adjourned for luncheon.
EVIDENCE FOR THE DEFENCE. MAJOR WILKINSON'S CAREER-GALLANTRY
IN souTa AFRICA.

On resuming, witnesses for the defence were called. John Frederick Kiernan, secretary of the Patten Arms Hotel, testified to the Major's accident in the hunting field. Dr. Henry Edward Gough, of Northwich, said he at- tended the Major after the accident in March of last year. The effect of concussion upon a man's brain was to leave it more susceptible to any irritation. In reply to Mr. Gill witness said the Major would be more sus- ceptible to the effect of alcohol. Colonel Thiele, of the Rayal Army Medical Corps said Major Wilkinson was under his care between the 30th March and 4th April last. He was then on the sick list, suffering from influenza. In his opinion the Major had not gone on the sick-list soon enough. It was quite possible for concussion to render a man more susceptible to the influence of alcohol. Captain George A. Brush, of the King's Liverpool Regiment, said he was in the regiment when Major Wilkinson joined it in the West Indies in 1896. He was in the same battalion with the Major until after the relief of Ladysmith. They went through the seige together; and afterwards parted. During those four years Major Wilkinson was always strictly sober. Witness was with him at Aldershot, for a month this year and the Major had also stayed with him in Liver- pool. He was always strictly sober. Brevet Major Stephenson said Major Wilkinson was his subaltern during the South African war, when witness was commanding mounted infantry. The Major was always thoroughly sober, and witness considered him to be one of the best officers he had ever had under Captain L. M. Jones, Adjutant to the King's Liver- pool Regiment, gave similar evidence. Major Wilkin- son, he said, was promoted for conspicuous conduct in holding a post at Helvetia when the other two posts surrendered. Mr. Gill intimated that he had received a letter from Major Molyneux Seal who was unable to attend, but the Court refused to hear it read. Major-General F. G. Menders, step-father of the accused, said he had known Major Wilkinson practically all his life. Since returning from South Africa the Major had spent much time at witness's home, and they had visited Paris together. Witness had never seen him in any way the worse for liquor, nor had he ever' seen him with the slightest inclination to drink. This was the first time he had ever heard of anything of the kind happening. A ST RONG PLEA BY MR. GILL. Mr. Gill, in addressing the Court on behalf of the accused, said he was not there to justify Major Wilkin- son's conduct. On his behalf he desired to apologise and to repeat the apology he had already made to Captain Osborne. But regrettable as the Major's con- duct was, he would submit that it was open to question whether it properly came within the terms of the section of the Act, as being conduct which was to the prejudice both of good order and military discipline. He submitted that it was not a matter cognisable under that section. A very wide discretion appeared to be reposed in the Court in drawing the line as to what was pre- judicial to good order and discipline. He noticed that inthe army manual it was pointed out that regard must betaken of the conduct itself and to the circumstances under which it took place. With regard to the charge of drunkenness, that was 'a matter which must vary greatly in its gravity. A man might be unconscious in drink; he might be unable to speak; he might be staggering in his gait; on the other hand he might be merely excited by liquor. He had heard it said that a man was drunk because his judgment was impaired or again drunkenness in the army meant,when a man was not fit for duty. If such a wide construction was put upon it he supposed it would be difficult for him (counsel) to contend on the evidence that Major Wilkinson did not come within the scope of the charge, because he would not deny that Major Wilkinson had been greatly excited by the wine that he had drunk, and so his judgment was impaired. Probably Major Wilkinson did not realise the extent to which the wine had taken hold of him. He (Mr. Gill) would submit in regard to the charge of intoxication that it was not by any means a serious case. The powers of the court were very extended. It was provided that if an officer or soldier were convicted of drunken- ness he should on conviction be liable to be cashiered, or the Court could exercise alternative powers, such as forfeiture, in tjie prescribed manner of seniority, a reprimand or a severe repremand. The court was em- powed to pass one or other of these sentences and they had also the right to couple with their sentence a recommendation to mercy. It was a case in which a very lenient construction might be put upon the con- duct of Major Wilkinson and he was entitled to the merciful consideration of the Court. About a year ago, Major Wilkinson had a fail from his horse and falling upon his head, he suffered from concussion. It was a matter of common knowledge that where a man had sustained a very severe shock he was liable to feel the effects of it for some time afterwards. His nervous system was less strong and he was more suscep- tible to the influence of alcohol than he was before. It was further to be remarked that very shortly before- the unfortunate episode on the 19th of April, Major Wilkinson had an attack of influenza and was suffering from the effects of it. A man in that condition was more likely to be affected by a moderate quantity of alcohol than under ordinary circumstances. Proceeding to refer to the remark made by Major Wilkinson, Mr. Gill said a great deal of artificial import- ance had been attached to it. He daresay there were few men who had reached the age of 40 years who could look back and say, never in the whole course of their careers had they taken a little too much champagne a dinner. He daresay there were officers who after transt grossing in that way,had afterwards served their country and deserved well of it. Mr. Gill Ihen commented on Captain Osborne's conduct and said great excuse ought to be made for the conduct of Major Wilkinson at the moment. The assault was committed under cir- cumstances of great provocation and an exaggerated importance had been given to it. He would ask the court to remember that the accused had already Suffered in regard to the charge, as he had been under arrest for something like six weeks. Mr. Gill proceeded to refer to the good services rendered to the country by the accused. He was but 27 years of age. That was perhaps too young an age for his rank. It would probably have been better for him if he had not been so distinguished and if he had had to wait for his promotion. At an earlylage he went through the siege of Ladysmith, and for an act of gallantry at Helvetia he was promoted to the rank of brevet-major at the earliest possible moment Counsel concludes by asking the court to take into consideration the extenuating circumstances and also the provocation Major Wilkinson received at the time of the assault. If the court were of opinion that the accused was guiliy, he submitted it was a case of which they might take a very lenient' view indeed, and still leave to the Sovereign of this country the services of one who had been a very distinguished officer in the stress of action. The decision of the court will be promulgated at a later date.

Mission Work in Brittany. Academy-street Chapel was filled on Wednesday evening with a congregation that had asseMbied to hear some account of Protestant mission work in Brittany from the lips of Pasteur and Madame Le Coat. Mr. Henry Eyes presided and briefly introduced tine Brittany pastor and his wife. The address of Pasteur Le Coat was delivered in brokelP English but he succeeded in making himself understood. The people of Brittany, he said, had a language of their own, which was distinct from the French language. They were kept in darkness, superstition and ignor- ance, largely owing tn the influence of the Roman Catholic Church. The speaker proceeded to speak of his efforts to revise the Bible in the Brittonic language, and to the success which had attended its distribution amongst the people by colporteurs. The early beginnings of Protestant mission St ork in Brittany were described,and despite many difficulti es,he said,the work was advancing.--Madame Le Coat very fluently described her work amongst the children She had established homes for orphan boys and giris,a hospital and dispensary, and also schools for boys and girls. All these institutions had been paid for, but she wished to raise funds to extend the work. She started her orphanage with five or six children and now she had sixty little ones under her care. She appealed for assistance in extending this eminently Christian work. —Mr. Joseph Twigs addressed the gathering and said they had all been deeply interested in hearing of the Protestant mission work which Pasteur and Madame Le Coat had started in Brittany. He was sure many Warrington friends would be pleased to assist in extending the work in this near mission field. A collection was taken at the close on behalf of the Mission.

The Coroner said the question for the jury to decide was whether the affair was a pure accident, or whether they thought it came about through some defect in the machinery. He did not like something being done after the accident and before the inquiry, especially when everybody fought so shy of telling them anything about the wotk. It did not leave a good taste in one's mouth. The Foreman: It makes it look bad on the face of the thing, to take the photo after it had been altered. After deliberating in private, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death" but attached blame to the firm for "not seeing that the machines were kept in proper order. and for allowing the set screws to project." The Coroner: I suppose you agree that it would have been far better if the photo had been taken of the machine just as it was, and not after they had remedied it.
The Foreman: Yes. It looks as if they had been trying to hide something. . . - -

We fonnd the defect, remedied it, and put the man on." If they had said that we should never have said a word to them

It is not fair, and if the officials of this town are to be hampered in their duty in this way you will have to double or treble your staff.
