WARRINGTON TRADERS AND THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY. The three trading firms—Messrs. Monks Hall and Company, James Fairclough and Sons, and Joseph Cros- field and Sons—who petitioned against the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, all obtained clauses for their special .protection. These protective clauses are as follow : FOR PROTECTION OF' MESSRS. MONKS HALL AND COMPANY, LIMITED. In addition to the provisions of the Section of this Act whereof the marginal note is "For protection of Corporation and Traders of Warrington "the following provisions for the protection of Messrs. Monks Hall and Company Limited or other the owner or owners far the time being of their works and premises situate at Warrington (in this Section called "the owners") shall be observed and have effect : (1) In the application of the provisions of sub- Section (9) of the hereintofore-mentioned Section of this Act to the owners' wharf (four hundred feet in length)opposite to their tube works the period of seven days shall be substituted for the period of two months referred to in the said sub-Section and all dredging at the said wharf in pursuance of that Section shall when commenced be carried on continuously so as to clear the said wharf as quickly as possible. (2) The Company shall pay compensation to the owners for any loss of quay space and water frontage and for severance resulting from the exercise of the powers conferred by this Act and in case or difference the amount of such compensation shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of the 'Lands Clauses Acts with reference to the settlement of questions of disputed compensation in the case of the purchase of lands otherwise than by agreement. Provided that in estimating the amount of such compensation regard shall be had to the benefit accruing to the owners by 'reason of the use by them for wharf purposes of the I dam (Work No. 6) by this Act authorised as in the next succeeding sub-Section provided which shall be fairly estimated and set off against the said compensations (3) The Company shall permit the owners to use the dam (Work No. 6) for wharf purposes and shall con- struct and maintain along the south face of such dam and for a length of 100 feet a suitable staging to admit of such user subject to the right of way of the Com- pany across the said data to the towing path. Provided that the owners shall so use the said darn for wharf purposes as not to cause any interference with the working of the culverts and sluices therein or connected therewith. (4) The Company shall pay compensation to the owners for the loss or injury (if any) which may be ascertained to be due to delay occasioned to the vessels of the owners or vessels chartered by them by reason of the exercise of any of the powers conferred by this Act. In case of difference the amount of such com- pensation shall be determined ,by arbitration under the provisions of "The Arbitration Act, 1889." FOR PROTECTION OF MESSRS. JAMES FAIRCLOUGH AND SONS. In addition to the provisions of the Section of this Act whereof the marginal note is "For protection of Corporation and Traders of Warrington " the following provisions for the protection of ,Messrs James Fair- dough and Sons Limited or other the °vier or owners for the time being of the Mersey Mills and Bank Quay Mills Warrington (in this Section called "the owners") shall be observed and have effect : (1) In the application of the provisions of sub- Section (9) of the hereinbefore mentioned Section of this Act to the owners' crane wharf (one hundred feet in length) at Bank Quay Mills the period of seven days shall be substituted for the period of two months re- ferred to in the said sub-Section and all dredging at the said wharf in pursuance of that Section shall when commenced be carried on continuously so as to clear the said wharf as quickly as possible: (2) The Company shall not commence the construc- tion of Work No. 6 by this Act authorised until they have paid compensation to the owners for the loss of water power at their Mersey Mills as if in consequence of the exercise of the powers of this Act the owners were entirely deprived of all water power at such Mills and in case of difference the amount of such compensa- tion shall be determined in accordance with the provi- sions of the Lands Clauses Acts with reference to the settlement of questions of disputed compensation in the case of the purchase of lands otherwise than by agreement and upon payment of such compensation the owners thall assign their rights of water power at the ' said Mills to the Company; (3) If and so long as the Company comply with the provisions of sub-Section (16) of the hereinbefore mentioned Section of this Act the owners shall not be entitled to any compensation for any diminution of headroom for their vessels when passing under Warring- ton Bridge which may result from the exercise of the powers conferred by this Act. FOR PROTECTION OF JOSEPH CROSFIELD AND SONS. In addition to the provisions of the Section of this Act whereof the marginal note is "For protection of Corporation and Traders of Warrington" the follow- ing provisions for the protection of Messrs Joseph Crosfleld and Sons, Limited, or other the owner or owners for the time being of their Works and premises situate at Warrington (in this Section called "the owners ") shall be observed and have effect ; *(1) In the application of the provisions of sub-sec- tion (9) of thehereinbefore mentioned section of this Act to the owners' wharf two hundred and forty• feet in length) opposite to their warehouse the period of seven days shall be substituted for the period of two months referred to in the said sub-Section and all dredging at the said wharf in pursuance of that Section shall when commenced be carried on continuously so as to clear the said wharf as quickly as possible. (2) If on the thirteenth day of May one thousand nine hundred and four there is a right of access for cart traffic to the new land acquired or agreed to be acquired by the owners opposite to their existing Works at or near Bank Quay the Company shall during the construc- tion of the river diversion (Work No. 5) by this Act authorised afford to the owners the best temporary access to the said land for such traffic as may be reasonably practicable and on the com- pletion of the said work shall in perpetuity afford to the owners a right of access to' the said land for such traffic either by means of a bridge across the said river diversion in such position as the Company may determine or (if the same can be arranged by the Company) from some public carriage- road across the dam (Work No. 6) by this Act authorised and such bridge or other means of access shall at all times be capable of bearing a load of ten_ tons.

Baptismal Service at Hill Cllffe. The Baptist Chapel was filled on Sunday evening, on the occasion of a Baptismal service. The pastor the Rev. J. S. Hughes occupied the pulpit, and special hymns were sung. Mr. Hughes took as his text, Exod xii, 26. "What mean ye by this service ?" Using these words as his motto he explained very fully why Baptists differed from other Christians in the administration of the ordinance of Baptism, giving as his reasons their desire to be loyal to the sacred scriptures, loyal to the demand of Christ, and loyal to their personal convic- tions. The sermon was listened to with great attention, and the ordinance administered in the most solemn manner, and .the impression produced was such that at the close four others offered themselves as candidates

lof Druids, and during that period he has made. three ;valuations of the whole district; revised the rules and introduced a new system of keeping the lodge registers. whereby the work has been greatly facilitated and improved throughout the ten lodges comprising the district.. Mr. Houghton's third valuation of the dis- trict reveals an increased value of the last five. years of ss. per member. Some years ago it was felt by the officers that Mr. Houghton's valuable !services deserved special recognition and it was decided to present him with the titles of past district master and past district grand master, and also with an illuminated address and certificate of merit. Mr. Houghton's connection with the Druids dates back to 1875 and he has always taken a deep interest in the society's welfare. From the first he has been officially cm- nected with the Order and he has held most of the positions connected with it, including those of lodge secretary and lodge treasurer. About 11 years ago he started the Penketh United Lodge, and in order that he might the more effectively use his influence on its behalf, he applied for his transfer to it, which was granted. The lodge has now over 100 members and much of its success is due to the energy of Mr. Houghton. It will be remembered that Hr. Houghton successfully discharged the onerous duties of hon. secretary of the Friendly Societies Procession Com- mittee in celebration of the Coronation of the King. The procession was originally fiked to take place on June 26th, 1902, but o xing to the serious indisposi- tion of the King, the procession to the great regret of all concerned, had to be postponed until August. Mr. Houghton took a prominent part in the inauguration of the Warrington Friendly Societies Council, and-he now holds the honoured position of President.

div.head: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MRS. PETER STUBS.
div.p: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MRS. PETER STUBS.

We record with deep regret the death, which took placelate on Friday night last, of Isabella, wife of Mr. Pater Stubs, of Blaisdon Hall, Gloucestershire. Mrs. Stubs was 76 years of age, and she had been enjoying very excellent health of late. She was in her dressing room on the morning of the 16th, when she was seized. with a stroke. Dr. Searancke was in immediate attend- ance, and other medical help was summoned, but the case was hopeless from the first, and death occurred as stated. The terrible grief of the family was shared by the villagers, who were greatly distressed on learning that Mrs. Stubs illness had had a fatal termination. The family came into Gloucestershire from Warring- ton some 15 years ago, and soon began to make many friends, and earned and secured the respect of the parishioners•and the people generally. Mrs. Stubs dis- pensed her wealth without ostentation, but her benefac- tions were large and general and continuous, and she was certainly regarded as the Lady Bountiful of the parish and for miles outside it. In her death the villagers have lost a kind and sympathetic friend, one whose place it will be very difficult to fill, and it is not surprising that many should come to regard her decease as one of the greatest calamities that could befall them. The funeral took place at noon On Wednesday, the place of interment being Blaisdon Churchyard. some 300 yards from the mansion. An earth grave had been prepared, but the sides of this and the turf arounct it were carefully laid with moss,andan abundance of beau- tiful white blooms, ivy leaves, laurel, lilac, arum lilies, 6:e. The corpse was contained in an elm shell, lined' with silk. The outer case was of solid English oak, french polished, massive brass furniture, and the name plate contained the following : "Isabella Stubs died May 20th, 1904, aged 76 years. The Rector of the parish, Rev. Douglas Jones offici- ated throughout, and there was no departure from the simple prayer book burial service, there being no music or singing: The chancel Seats were laden with a magni- ficent array Of floral emblems, the odour from which permeated the whole atmosphere of the sacred edifice. The mourners were Mr. Stubs,(husband) Mrs. Ma,clver, and Mrs. Waters (daughters), Rev. Greenall, (brother), Captain Waters, and Mr. Maclver, (sons-in-law), Colonel Godfrey, Mr. R. Frost, Mr. H. Greenall, and Mr. R. Fenton (nephews), together with Miss Robinson, (Mrs. Stubs' maid), Alice Hewett, Maud Bradford, and Mrs. Baxter, (indoor servants). Other relatives attending the service at the Church were Mr. and Mrs. Frost, Mr. Aylmer Frost, Mr. J. G. Frost, Mrs. R. Frost, Mr. Henry Greenall, whilst there were also presentithe following : Mr. and Mrs. W. C. Nigel Jones, Mr. and Mrs. R. J. Kerr (the Hall), Mr. T. Alger, Rev. F. J. Fulford, Mr. and Mrs. M. W. Bennett, Mrs. Peril- berthy, Mr. A. Short, Mr. D. Parslow and Mr. Job Rudge. The labourers on the estate with their wives, also attended the service. I The under-bearers, watkmen on the estate were as follow: J. Perkins, P. Williams, F. Clarke, J. Ingham G. Rutter and W. Preston. The wreaths were a very costly and beautiful array oflowers,and they were sent, on behalf of the undermentioned.—The family at Blais- don Hall, Captain and Mrs. Waters, Mr. and Mrs. Collin Maclver, Miss Alline and Ruth Maclver9 Mr. and Mrs. Trafford Huteson, Mr. and Mrs. Tevv, Lady Frost, Mrs. Barretts, Leonard J. div.head: CURIOUS SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASE.
div.p: CURIOUS SCHOOL ATTEND- ANCE CASE.
A PARENT AND HIS MEDICAL CERTIFICATE.
Education Committee has to Withdraw.

A school attendance prosecution which raised some interesting points was heard at the Warrington Police Court yesterday when Mr. William Anford Proud, 23, Lovely-lane, was summoned for neglecting to send his child Elsie to school.—Mr. Stanley Wilson. deputy town clerk, prosecuted on behalf of the Education Com- mittee,and Mr. A Browne defended.

Mr. 'Wilson said that. as the magistrates were probably aware the defendant held an important public appoint- ment in the town. During the house-to-house visitation of one of the school attendance inspectors it was found on April sth that defendant's daughter Elsie, aged five years, was not attending any school. The inspector saw Mrs. Proud, who said the child was in a delicate state' of health and unable to go to school. The inspector' told her it would be necessary to supply a doctor's certificate, and Mrs. Proud said she had one in her possession, and if he would call again she would pro- duce it. Me called again on May 4th and Mrs. Proud said she had not found the certificate and requested him to call again. On making another visit on the 9th he was told by Mrs. Proud that she would have nothing further to do with him, and that he must see Mr. Proud. On the following day he saw Mr. Proud who promised to see the Director of Education. Subse- quently Mr. Proud saw the Director who wrote two letters, the first reminding him that he had not re- ceived the certificate and the second that he had not received a reply to his previous letter. The case came :before- the committee, and they ordered a third letter to be sent, intimating that unless the certificate was produced before the 19th inst? proceedings would be taken. In- reply Mr. Proud wrote to the Director : "On awl after Tuesday next I shall be at home. and if you will instruct your officer to call any afternoon, except Wednesday, about 2.30, I shall be pleased* to shocv him the doctor's certificate. This offer has been previously made to him, but he declined it." The letter was brought before the com- mittee who ordered a. prosecution. They felt it was a deliberate case in' which they had been set at defiance, and their officers had' been-caused needless trouble. Up to the present time. no- certificate had been handed in. Ire (Mr. Wilson) understood one would be produced that morning, and that the Bench-would haven° alterna- tive but to dismiss the case. The committee felt they should receive the support of the Bench in a case of that kind. If it had not been for the consideration the committee had shown, to the position Mr. Proud held, the case would have been brought into Court before. William Farrar, school attendance inspector, was then called.
Mr. Browns: Mr. Wilson has actually opened for a dismissal.
Mr. •Mr Wilson You have. handed me a certificate. _ - ._. _ _

Mr. Browne: Whit, is th 3 use of go-ini-On7vlt-h- it.? Why not withdraw. You have seen a most serious certi- ficate given by a leading specialist of Liverpool and yet you insist on going on. Mr. Wilson: I insist on going on. Mr. Browne: It is simply for exposure and nothing else. It is nothing but revenge. Mr. Wilson: The certificate has not yet been put in. Mr. Browne has shown it to me, and' on the face of that certificate a conviction cannot take place. But look at the trouble the Education Committee and their officers have been put to in attending this morning, entirely in consequence of the defendant's stubbornness. I think I am entitled to costs.

Mr. Browne: We had anotfier certificate previously from Dr. Peter Stuart, of Liverpool. We are not bound to produce it. If you will show me any law to say that we are bound to come to the Education Office to pro- duce it, lain give way.

Mr. "Wilson If they won't produce it, the only course is to bring them to the Court. Mr. Browne: My friend has read a letter offering to show the certificate if they called at the house. Mr. Wilson: And they calledsix. times. Mr. Browne:He had always been willing and ready to producelit.He has been to the oqce once,but was arossly insulted by a deputy of Mr. Moore Murray. He was told in fact that he (the deputy) did not believe he had a certificate.

Mr. Wilson: I don't think that is quite fair. Mr. Browne: As a public townsman, Mr. Proud is not going to be insulted by new public officials. Mr. Wilson: lam prepared to call Mr. Roberts, the gentleman referred to, if necessary. It is not fair to make a statement of that kind.

Mr. H. Roberts: What is the duty of a parent with regard to the production of a certificate. Assuming the school attendance officer calls in the usual way is it the duty of the parent to produce to him a certificate? Mr. Wilson: Undoubtedly. Mr. Browne: But can you show us that by any authority?
Mr. Wilson : The defendant has acted in a most stubborn way throughout, and has set the committee at defiance.
Mr. Browne: We hive done nothing of the kind. Mr. Wilson: Are you willing to pay costs if we with- draw it?
Mr. Browne : No.

Mr. Farrar then proceeded with his evidence bearing out Mr. Wilson's statement. He said no certificate had been received in proof of Mr. Proud's statement. Mr. Wilson: What is the rule? Mr. Browne: That is not the question. What is the law?

Mr. Wilson: The law is that every chiid not less than live and not more than fourteen years of age shall attend school unless—and there are three reasons given. The one we rely upon is "When a child has been pre- vented from attending school by sickness or any other unavoidable cause." It is for the defendant to satisfy the School Attendance Committee that the case comes within that sub-section.
Mr. Browne : That is only your argument. Alderman Smethurst: And you carry that out do you? ,

Mr. Wilson: Certainly: in every case. Alderman Smethurst: You find hundreds of children running about the streets never spoken to, and you bring respectable people here. Incross-examination, Mr. Farrar said Mrs. Proud told him that her husband had the certificate.

Mr. Browne: On meeting Mr. Proud, did you tell him you did not believe he hada certificate. Witness: No, sir. Mr. Browne: Weren't you most insulting? Witness: No, sir. Mr. Browne: Didn't Mr. Proud walk away from you in consequence of your insulting him? Witness: No, sir. Mr. Browne: Did you report to Mr. Roberts or Mr. Murray that you did not believe he had a certificate? Witness : No. sir.
Further questioned, witness admitted that he fre- quently passed the Savings Bank, where Mr. Proud was the actuary, but he had not called to see him.
Mr. Brotvne: It is coming to this isn't it? There has been some friction between the director of the Education Committee and the managers of St. BArnabas' school.
Witness: Not to my knowledge. Mr. Browne: Is not that the reason why you were advised not to go to the bank to see Mr. Proud who had the certificate in his pocket?

Witness: No, sir. Mr. Browne: Who advised you ant to go to the bank? Witness: My superiors at the office. Mr. Browne: Who are your superiors? Witness: Mr. Bamber, Mr. Roberts, and Mr:Murray. Further cross-exarnined witness said he believed what Mr. Proud said about the child being delicate, but it was his duty to ask for a, certificate. _ _

Mr. BroNc;ne: What did you want a doctor's certifi- cate for when a man in Mr. Prond's position told you he had paid a doctor's bill of .£l6 for attendance on the child during the past few months? Mr. H. Roberts: I don't think you can expect the officers to take any man's word. Itappears to me this is a storm in a teacup. lam rather surprised that any gentleman in Mr. Proud's position shoulii not think it worth his while to send the certificate by post or to personally call and explain. Mr. Browne: My client did call. Mr. Wilson : He has refused to supply a certificate up to this point. The Mayor (who presided) : It seems to me it is a matter of red-tape. I think the officials might have seen Mr. Proud, got an explanation, and been satisfied. Mr. H. Roberts: And then you have people saying there is one law for the rich, and another for the poor. Alderman Smethurst: There is in this case. Re-examined, witness said the Savings Bank was not in his district. It was not usual to visit people at their places of business. Mr. J. Moore Murray, Director of Education, then entered the witness-box. _ _
At this stage It was intimated that only Mr. H. Roberts and Mr. Hepherd intended to adjudicate in the

div.head: HONOUR FOR A WARRINGTON DAUID.
div.p: HONOUR FOR A WARRINGTON DAUID.
Mr. Houghton Elected Vic-Grand
Master of the Order.

At the annual delegation of -the Order of Druids, held at Oswestry on Wednesday, Mr. David Houghton who is president of the Warrington Friendly Societies Council, was elected to the office of Vice-Grand Master by a majority of 9711 votes. There were three candi- dates for the office, namely Mr. David Houghton of Warrington, Mr. Charles W. Shipp of Bristol, and Mr. Charles Kent, of Sheffield. The choice of the delega- tion fell on Mr. Houghton, by the substantial majority stated. Mr. Houghton was a candidate for the posi- tion a year ago, but was defeated by Mr. R. H. Mason, of Oswestry, who is the grand master for the ensuing year. In accordance with a long-standing custom, the vice-grand master is promoted to the position of grand master in the following year after his election, so that a year hence, Mr. Houghton will have the distingoishei honour of occupying the highest position in the Order he has so devotedly served for a long number of years. A few particulars with reference to Mr. Houghton's connection with Druidism will not be out of place. The new Vice-Grand Master has for manylvears occupied a seat on the Board of Management of the Order, where his ripe experience and keen business instincts have been of the greatest value. For nearly eight years,he has also held the important office of district corres- ponding secretary for the Warrington District Society

div.head: SCENE AT AN INQUEST. The Fatality at Vulcan Foundry.
div.p: SCENE AT AN INQUEST. The Fatality at Vulcan Foundry.
EMPLOYERS BLAIMED.

There was a " scene " at the inquiry conducted at Warrington on Tuesday by Mr. S. Brighouse, County Coroner, into the circumstances attending the death of William Wharton, (41), of 260, Wafgrave-road, Earles- town, who was fatally injured whilst following his em- ployment at the Vulcan Foundry, Earlestown. Mr. A. Lewis, H.M. Inspector of Factories, watched the pro- ceedings on behalf of the Home Office. George Henry Wharton, deceased's brother, who is also employ ed at the foundry,said that at eight o'clock on Thursday morning of last week deceased was engaged at a drilling machine "counter sinking." Witness was working at the next machine. Hearing ashout,he looked round and saw the deceased lying by the side of the machine. Assistance was at hand, and after deceased had been seen by Dr. Mouncey, he was removed to the Warrington Infirmary where he died from a fractured spine. Witness was of the opinion that the side screw or nipple of the machine caught deceased's "slap," which was new, and he was dragged round the machine. In answer to the coroner witness said he did not think there was any serious danger in working at the drilling machines, although there was a likelihood of the manipulator's clothes being caught if he stood too near. The Coroner: You are supposed to have your slop , buttoned up. Witness: You are supposed to do, but it is in the way sometimes if it is fastened. Mr. Lewis question,,d the witness at some length. Witness admitted that since the accident the set screw had been taken out of his machine but he could not say what had been done to the socket. Previously the set screw had projected half an inch. Mr. Lewis: Isn't there an unwritten rule that the set screws have to be " flush " with the face of the socket? Witness: I have not seen one, that lam aware of. Further questioned witness said deceased's clothing had been so twisted round the machine,that he (witness) could not see what part had been caught. Mr. Ritchie, the assistant manager at the works, said it was an unwritten rule that no projecting set screws should be used. Cases had come to the knowledge of the firm in which men had obtained other set screws, unknown to the authorities, and used tbena. If any- thing went wrong with the set screws, the men ought to go to the millwrights' shop. In answer to Mr. Lewis, witness stated that since the accident a new screw had been put into the socket of the machine. Asked who gave instructions for the work to be done he said the instructions would go to the millwright's shop. Mr. Lewis commented upon the fact that a photo- graph, produced for the guidance of the Coroner and jury, did not show the machine as it was at the time of the accident, but as it appeared without a projecting set screw. The Coroner: The suggestion is that since the acci- dent happened you have done something to the machine. You evidently found out what was the cause of the accident and remedied it before the Inspector visited the works. Mr. Ritchie: lam not aware that that has been done, but lam aware that if .there was any projecting set screw on the machine, it would be altered before we put another man on. Mr. Lewis: All the machines have been attended to since the accident. The Coronet: Why don't you tell us who found it out and who has remedied it? Mr. Ritchie: I am perfectly candid about that. There has been a definite order given to the millwright's department that no set screws be allowed to project. There has been an order for years past. When the acci- dent occurred it was thought that a projecting setscrew might have contributed to the accident, anda special order was given for the machines to be examined. Alfred Hayes, foreman, said that after the accident. deceased told him that it was the point of the drill and not the set screw that caught him. The set screws of the machines had now been shortened by the millwrights. The Coroner: By whose order? Witness: The millwrights would know from their past experience that the screws should be flush. The Coroner (warmly): You are all trying to hum- bug me, but I won't be humbugged. lam going to find out all about it, and I will adjourn the inquiry if you don't help me. I have sat here for twenty years. You are trying to deceive the inspector and, myself. Some one has gone round and found out the cause of the acci- dent. You have shut the stable door after the horse, has gone, mid no one will tall me about it. You will have to tell me or come here again. Go back and talk to your master and make up your mind what you are going to say in the box, or else I will adjourn the inquiry. Mr. Ritchie: We have no wish- The Coroner: Something has been done at the works since the accident happened. I want to know who did it, and by whose order. Mr. Ritchie: I have been perfectly candid. The Coroner: You have not been so far. No one is candid with me so far. Mr. Ritchie: Our works manager gave orders that the machines were to be examined, immediately after the accident. The Coroner: Is he here? Mr. Ritchie : No. The Coroner: Who carried out his orders? Mr. Ritchie : Our millwright foreman. The Conner: Is he here? Mr. Ritchie : No, sir, I never thought this question would have arisen. The Coroner: I don't take it as a compliment to me. Mr. Ritchie: I have done everything I thought would be required. Mr. Lewis said he visidxl the works that day. The notice received from thelfirm simply stated thatideceased's jacke was caught by the drilling machine spindle. He was told that the machine was precisely in the same condition as it was at the time of the accident. On examining it he found that the set screw was quite flush and that the recess had recently been deepened. The gentleman who showed him round could not tell him by whose orders the work had been done. He (Mr. Lewis) concluded that the information would be forth- coming at the inquest. He examined two machines close by,one of which was worked by deceased's brother. The set screws were quite flush, but there was no evi- dence of anything having been done to the recesses. He

div.head: LYMM MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL.
div.p: LYMM MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL.
REVELS CUT SHORT BY RAIN.

Lymm is on of those old-work/ places where it seems quite the natural thing to hold May revels. Quaintness and rustic beauty make a charming .setting• to pretty pageantry and ceremonial, and it is little wonder that the people take a pride in their annual crowning of the Queen of the May. On this day of days the village throws off its wonted serenity, and gaiety and animation hold sway.. By train, brakes, bicycles and a host of vehicles the visitors come in their hundreds—and Warrington always sends its fair quota. When the crowds began to muster in the old streets for Thursday's festival—which was the fifteenth of its kind—Lymm, bathed in glorious sunshine, was looking at its best. Gratifying success, it was felt, must crown the efforts of those who had willingly given their time to the work of preparation. Unfortunately,. the delusiveness of English sunshine had once more to- be brought home to visitors and villagers alike. The assembling of the procession attracted a large concourse round the village cross—in fact the ancient landmark itself was seized upon as a place of vantage. Wherever one. turned there was a sea of fao39, and here and there a mass of cplour denoted the arrival of some ne w feature of the pageant. Everything in order, a verse of the National Anthem was sung, and the march round the village commenced.

div.head: PRETTY PAGEANT.
div.p: A PRETTY PAGEANT.

-•-• Pretty indeed was the pageant, although there was little of the strikingly elaborate. At the head was the Lymm and Oughtrington Silver band playing lively airs, and children of the Congregational Sunday School and Band of Hope followed. The three beautifully decorated cars representing the United Kingdom came in for a great deal of admiration. On the "England and %Vales " car was a pleasing arrangement of Gothic arches, decorated with red and white roses. The representative of England (Miss Annie Ratcliffe) was attired in a long white robe decked with roses, and there was a semi-circle of red roses over her head. Miss Mary Dawson, who represented Wales, wasprettily dressed in white and green, and played a harp. Huge thistles were con- spicuous in the representation of Scotland, there being one at each corner of the car. Miss Edna Jennings,who- was seated on a dais in the centre' was dressed in, pale heliotrope muslin. The sides of the car were neatly draped with muslin. Miss Mary Daniels was seated in the centre of the "Ireland" car. She was taste- fully gowned in green, and held a shamrock staff. The sides of the car were covered with large scalloped shamrocks, and the effect was artistic. There, was a host of characters in the procession, and some of the costumes were remarkably good. Prominent, figures in history were succeeded by personages famed in nursery lore. The promoters of the festival are nothing if notlup.to-datsandJapairese and Russian soldierT were seen fraternising as though war were unheard of.Of course, Oliver Cromwell was en cridenec, and the Black. Prince, mounted, was a "make-up" which attracted considerable attention. The judge, in wig and robe, was not stern enough to inspire feelings of awe in the little fairy who tripped along quite nc,ar him. Then there were diminutive soldiers and "members of the force," groups of dancers who afterwards went through their graceful movements ()lithe field,a couple of China- men, and little Geishas.

THE ROYAL CORTEGE was preceded by Cradleld's prize band. The May Queen (Miss M. J. Bradbury), wlio rode in an open carriage drawn by two greys, was becomingly dressed in cream cashmere, with a gathered silk yoke and front, and had a sweeping train of red velvet trimmed with swan's down. She carried a beautiful shower bouquet. Her train bearers were Willie Seymour and Arthur Reed. The maids of honour were Annie Rose, Selina Kennerley, Mabel Hewitt, Edith Goffin, Elizabeth Statham., and Nellie Taylor, who were attired in empire frocks of creani nun's veiling, trimmed with cream lace.. Their bouquets were, composed of narcissi, pink geraniums and maiden hair fern. Miss Annie Miller, who /fast year occupied the more exalted office, was the Rose Queen. She wore a pretty dress of cream alpaca strapped with satin, with a pink satin train; and carried a rose bouquet. On her head was a wreath of the same flower. She was attended by Elsie Miller and Maggie Hughes as maids of honour, and George Bell and George Goffin as train bearers. The rear of the procession was brought up by a cycling section which was not very well filled. Two notable characters were the snake charmer and the Bohemian Queen, and there was an ingenious model representing "Our navy." A "down at the heel" in- dividual who bore signs of rough usage wheeled a. dilapidated machine with the intimations "My first and last ride" and "'freak the news to Mother." Some terriblejdiscords were produced by " Flanagon's band from Strangeways "but the spectators bore the ordeal patiently. In fact they seemed not a little amused at the manoeuvres of the motley body of "instrumen- talists."

THE QUEEN CROWNED. • Bordered by tall, spreading trees, and commanding an extensive view of pretty, country, the football field" was an ideal spot for the crowning ceremony. Thither spectators wended their way in hundreds, and the coron- ation was enacted with fitting pomp. Amid the plaudits of the assembly the Queen was escorted to the throne. Then the crown bearer (James Struthers) advanced slowly, and frequently paused Ito do obeisance. The diadem was handed to Mrs. Mumford, who placed it up- on the head of the young queen, and the band played the Natioaail Anthem. Mrs. Mumford madea gift to" Her Majesty " of a book of Tennyson's poems. The sceptre bearer (James Jones) then pre- sented the emblem of authority, and the Corona- tion ceremonial was at an end. This was the signal for the revels to begin. The :loyal Maypole dance—of which the spectators never seem to weary— was cleverly danced by lads and lassies in old-time 1 costumes, and the ribbons were quickly plaited and as quickly unloosed. Fermi, a skilful wire walker, per- formed astonishing feats, and the Bros. Lloddge proved themselves athletes of no mean ability. A new dance, which gave infinite pleasure, wag the Old English dance, a number of girls dressed in green and white going through the movements in a way which reflected credit upon themselves and their nstructress.
RALN _CUTS THE RF.VELS SHORT.

By this time, the weather—so promisinC;a:littletarlier —had undergone a complete change. Clouds obscured the sun, end rain began to fail heavily. A coon dance was performed amid a perfect deluge but in praise of the youngsters it must be said that they went through their parts admirably. The interest of the spectators was retained, despite the discomfort which they were enduring, and hearty applause rewarded the entertainers' efforts. As the rain showed no signs of abating tha revels were brought to an abrupt close, and in almost as short a time as it takes to relate the field was cleared. Many people at once made their way to the station, and trains for' Warrington and district were filled. Not a few cyclists who had ridden to the village under such delightful conditions, chose to return by rail rather than brave the elements. Fortunately the rain cleared ^ off after tea, and an interesting variety programme was submitted. The bands supplied musics for dancing, and considering the climatic eccentricities of the afternoon, the festival may be regarded as a. success. The gratifying feature was that the attend- ance at the crowning ceremon3. did not suffer, and the promoters had no cause for anxiety on that score.

WORKERS. It would be difficult tb speak too highly of the ser- vices rendered by the bend of officials who threw them- selves whole-heartedly into the work. Mr. James D. B. Smith was an indefitigable secretary, and seemed to be here there and everywhere directing operations. Nor must we omit to mention the work of Miss Raper and Miss Madge Raper who were responsible for the danc- ing• of the children in general, and of Miss Winterburn, of Manchester, who had trained the girls for the Old English dance. The following is a list of the officials:— President, Mr. C. Raper; vice-president, Mr. R. H. Gotobed ; chairman, Mr. J. Hardy Holt; 111. C., Mr. E. Mumford ; hon. treasurer, :qr. George Willan ; hon. secretary, Mr. James D.B. Smith. Ladies' Committee: President, Miss West: hon. sec. Mrs. James D. B. Smith. Committee: Mesdames see., Gotobed,Holt, Leather, Porter, Simpson, and Smith, Misses Green, Heesom, Hesketh, E. Hesketh,Leah,Mcintyre,McLellan, Miller, Porter, Raper, M. Raper, Sutton West, Messrs. H. Thomas, P. Ardern, W. Ardern, Bradburn, J. Hewitt, A. Leather, Marr, W. G. Porter, M. Raper, Simpson, and A. Sutton.

div.head: UNITAIIRN MIN ISTER'S STIPENDS. Mr. F. Monks Suggests Female Students.
div.p: UNITAIIRN MIN ISTER'S STIPENDS. Mr. F. Monks Suggests Female Students.

"The supply of ministers for our churches" was a subject of discussion at the Unitarian Conference in. London yesterday. Mr. F. Monks, J.P., of Warrington, spoke of the diffi- culty of retaining ministers at that church on account of the higher stipend offered by richer churches. It was absurd to suppose that a Unitarian minister with a family and all its attendant responsibifities could afford to disregard the question of stipend. He did not so much mind the changes provided their colleges and institutions provided them. with equally good men, but this was not always the case, and the last two appointments at Warrington were of men who had not been specially trained for the Unit- arian ministry. He saw no reason why women should not be trained for the ministry, and he threw it out as a suggestion to the college authorities. The wretched stipends deterred many good men from taking up a noble and honourable calling. The stipends in many cases were not equal to the pay of an ordinary clerk, and even the so-called prizes of the profession were no better than the pay of a confidential clerk in a commercial establishment.

FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillors Roberts.and Thornton, Messrs. H. Roberts and Hepherd. THEFT OF SHEETS.—Margaret Tolly, Cropper'sißrow, was charged with stealing three sheets, the property of Winifred Connolly, Cropper's Brow—Prosecutrix left the house on May 15th, leaving the key with the prisoner in order that she could attend to the fire. When she returned the sheets were missing and prisoner had left her house. Superintendent Monaghan arrested her, and she said she was in drink when she committed the offence.—Prisoner, who made her 19th appearance, was sentenced to two months' hard labour. MINOR CASES.—Kate Dagnall, Bay Horse Yard, was sent to goal for 14 days for violently assaulting Mary Bowen, 12, Turner-street.—Harriet Wright, 19, Turner- street, was ordered to pay costs for an assault on Ellen Ridgway, 2, Turner-street.—lsaiah Elwell, 7, Barnard- street, was summoned for using threats towards Harry Walmsley, 42, Plumpton-street.—The case was dis- missed on payment of costs.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

A DESTRUCTIVE WARRINGTON WONI AN.—POLICE STATION WINDOW SMASHED. Annie Smith, a notorious character, appeared before the Warrington magistrates on Monday charged with wilfully breaking a pans of glassat the police buildings on Sunday night, doing damage to the extent of 15s.— The Chief Constable said the police had been annoyed for some time by the prisoner and one or two others of particularly destru:tive tendencies. As soon as these people came out of gaol or Workhouse one of the first things they did was to smash something. On Sunday night the prisoner deliberately threw a large stone through the superintendent's office window. She did that kind of thing repeatedly, and he asked the Bench to deal severely with her. It was a bitter shame that the ratepayers should have to keep her in gaol or in the Workhouse, and then have to make good the damage she did by her wariton mischievous tendencies. She had never done a week's work in her life.—Prisoner : What keeps me keeps you, and that's Government.—P.C. Leonard and another officer spoke to hearing a crash of glass, and on going outside they found the prisoner a law yards from the broken window. A large stone was found in the office.—Prisoner : Oh, go on. Give me what you can—six months—l can do that on my head.— The magistrates sentenced prisoner to two months' im- prisonment.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Cases.
SATCRDA.Y—Before_ Alderman Sutton. (in the chair)

and Mr. R. T. Fairclough. Two MONTHS Foa WIFE ASSAULT.—James McCarthy, 541, Knutsford-road, was charged on a warrant with having assaulted his wife, Mary Ellen McCarthy on the 17th May.—Complainant said that on the night of the 17th inst. prisoner got hold of her and threatened to throw her downstairs. Witness succeeded in preventing prisoner from doing this,and he struck her in the mouth making it bleed.—Prisoner said his wife commencedtbe "bother." She attempted to hit him with a poker, and if he had not warded off the blow, she would have " split . his head open." He had to put her down on the floor or she would have killed him.—Superintendent Monaghan said prisoner had previously been to gaol for neglecting his family, and he had also been before the court for wife assault.— Inspector ffickett gave the prisoner a bad character. He had heard the man threaten his wife and had seen himstrike her.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for two months with hard labour.—His wife was granted a separation order with 7s. per week alimony. ARREARS OF MAINTENANCE.—Fred Davies, 18, Victoria street, wts charged on a warrant with arrears of maintenance due to his wife amounting to £l. 12s.— Ile was orderel to pay the money at once or go to gaol for a month.

MONDAY—Before the Mayor (in the chair) Councillor Thornton and Mr. J. W. Hayward. DESTROYED HIS CLOTHES.—AIbert Smith, an inmate .of the Workhouse, was charged with destroying his clothes on Saturday. The evidence showed that the prisoner was admitted to the casual ward on Saturday night, having been three times within that week. At eight o'clock Mr. John Constable, the porter, went round the ward and found that prisoner had destroyed all his clothes. When asked why he had done so h said he wanted to belocked up and if they did not lock him up he would go outside, and break into a house.-- Prisoner said he tore the clothes up because they were not fit to wear.—He was sent to gaol for a month.
DNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. 114 Hayward (in the chair), and Mr. J. Geddes. _

SHOP-DOOR TitErr.—Mary Ann Leah, of no settled abode, was charged with stealing from the shop-door of Messrs. Dolan Bros., Hersemarket-street, a coat and -vest, of the value of 10s. 6d.—The evidence showed that the clothing was seen hanging at the door at a quarter to five on Tuesday. evening. Shortly afterwards Mr. George Makin, the manager, went to the door and saw prisoner walking away with the garments in her posses- sion. He tobk them from her, and informed P.C. Corbett who brought her to the Police Station.—Prisoner said she knew nothing about the matter, as she was under the influence of drink at the time.—Superintendent
MUSTARD.

div.head: ST. HELENS
div.p: ST. HELENS
AN UNDESIRABLE RECRUIT,

The St. Helens —Magistrates on Thursday remanded Joseph Canavan, to givehim an opportunity of enlist- ing. He was charged with assaulting his mother, an old wonan. It was stated that Canavan had only just come out of goal after serving six months for assault- ing her, and that he had previously served sentences of 28 days and 14 days for threatening her. In this case he was alleged to have knocked her down and to have followed her as she was going to the police station, nearly pushing her through a window.
"SPORTING HER. FIGURE."

Thomas Lynch,-;;;Ung married collier, of Ormskirk- road, Rainford, pleaded at St. Helens on Tuesday that he had a right to make things lively at Rainford at mid- night on the 12th inst., because his wife had been to St. Helens with another woman to the theatre, and had left her two young children in the house. The police said the man forced his way into the house of a woman and threatened them. They ran screaming down the lane. Lynch said his wife had been going about with a young widow named Beck or Webster, who had got £219 compensation on the death of her husband. She had "been sporting her figure" ever since, and had bought a gramophone, and attracted this man's wife to the house. He admitted that he had had some beer, and went home and got vexed.—Lynch was bound over to keep the peace.
