div.head: DEATH OF MR. WILLIAM DILLON.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. WILLIAM DILLON.
A Notable Footballer.

10:.3ath has this week removed a well-known ex-foot- baller of the Warrington team in the person of Mr. William Dillon, who has been landlord of the Raven Inn, Fennell-street, since the re-erection of that hostelry. Mr. Dillon was in his 42nd year, and may be said to have been cut off in his prime. He had been afflicted with pneumonia for some weeks, but no cause for alarm was felt until Sundav,when serious symptoms developed, and he ssea away on the following morning. In his footballing days he was one of the finest forwards who ever donned the jersey of the Warrington Club In 1887-8-9 he was the captain of the Warrington foot- ball team, and was one of the team which succeeded in carrying off the old South-West Lancashire Cup in the first year of its inauguration. In the season 1889-0 he also played in the whole of the Lancashire county matches. After his retirement from football he acted for many years as referee under Northern Union rules. He was always a loyal supporter of the War- rington club and whea he no longer chased the leather he rendered useful service as a member of the com- mittee. The news of his death came as a shock to his many friends. He leaves a widow and three children.
TRIBUTE FRONI THE AIEgBERS OF THE FOOTBALL CLUB.

At the annual meeting of the Warrington Football Club, held on Tuesday evening, a fitting tribute was paid to the memory of Mr. Dillon. Mr. H. ASHTON, hon. secretary, said it was with ,feel- ings of the deepest regret that he referred to the death of Mr. Dillon, their one time captain, and he was sure he was voicisg the wishes of the, whole of the members in so doing. Mr. Dillon was an old and faithful servant of the club and for a great number of years took a very close interest in its affairs. To work for it was to him truly a labour of love, and in the various high offices he had held he always proved himself an ardent and faithful official. Although for some years he had not taken an active part in the working of the club, his assistance could always be relied upon and was frequently given in maintaining the honour and welfare of the club. It was their duty as a club to pass a vote of condolence with his widow and family in their very great loss, and he moved a resolution to that effect. (Hear, hear.) The PRESIDENT (Mr. Neil) seconded, and said it was only fitting they should pay a tribute to Mr. Dillon's memory.
The motion was carried in silence, all standing. THE FUNERAL.

The grave closed over the remains of the late Mr. Dillon on Thursday afternoon when they were interred in the Warrington Cemetery. Notwithstanding the heavy rain which fell, a large number attended the last rites as a mark of respect. The coffin was borne to its last resting place by six ex-players of the Warrington team, all of them having been forwards in the team at the time of Mr. Dillon's captaincy of it. Their names are: John Rigby. Walter Povey, Fair Turner, H. Ashton T. Davies and Frank Turner. The Warrington Club was officially represented by Mr. Thomas Locker. The chief mourners present were : Beatrice, Annie and Dorothy Dillon (daughters), Mr. John Dillon Mr. Andrew Dillon and Mr. E. Dillon (brothers),Mr. Robert Webster and Mr. Joseph Massey (brothers-in-law), Mr. Andrew Plunkett (uncle). Amongst the general mourners were: Mr. Joseph Peacock, Mr. John Banner, Mr. Andrew Templeton, and Mr. Joseph Craik. The Licensed Victuallers' Association was represented by Messrs. Thomas Walsh secretary), Thomas Massey, Fred Clare, John McClinton, W. Partridge. Robert Walker, John Rigby, George Long,R. Perdue, Henry Teece, C. W. Newall, George Beard ansl H. Ashton. The Rev. Father Mercer impressively con- ducted the funeral service. A large number of floral tributes were sent, including one from the Warrington Football Club.

At Bridgend, on Wednesday, "Mr. Lloyd George said the Scottish people had made it clear a generation ago they would stand no clerical nonsense. The fight must be to place Wales side by side with Scotland. _

Miss A. Salisbury, of High Laver Schools, near Harrow,Essex, who arrived at Chackmore, near Bucking- ham, on Saturday evening, to take up her duties as schoolmistress, died in Northampton Infirmary on Wed- nesday as the remit of an accidental bullet wound. She was unpacking her boxes on Sunday in a cottage when she was struck by a bullet from a rifle with which some young men were shooting starlings in a garden outside.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May 28 1904
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 28 1904
MAGAZINE CLIPPINGS.
The French in Tunis.

The work of the French in Tunis has been wholly admirable. Contrary to their custom in Algeria, they have thought it wise to maintain a show of native sovereignty in the person of the Bey of Tunis; in fact, consciously or unconsciously, they have taken the same line in Tunis as we have followed in Egypt, with the same beneficial results. Hateful as it must always be to a proud Muhammadan people to see the Christian foreigner dominating the country. I begin to think that French rule in Tunis is actually becoming popular (which is a very strong thing to say,and which cannot be said about British rule in every one of our Muhammadan dependencies). I once asked a Berber of the south of Tunis .(who had fought hard against the French in 1881 but had since been allowed to return and settle down at his old home) what he thought was the greatest benefit that the French had conferred on the country. He re- plied promptly" Water," and pointed to the magnificent fountains that were spurting from artesian wells, and the irrigation channels glistening in all directions over a plain which was now a glorious garden of vegetation but which a few years ago had been hopeless, sandy desert. He and others went on to assure me that so deeply did the common people feel the boon the French had conferred on them (in cheap and abundant water) that they had begunto love them. In Tunis,moreover, the old Turkish government of Beys was detested by the Arabs and Berbers, and, foreigner for foreigner,the y prefer the Frenchman to the Turk.—From "The French Empire in North Africa and the Anglo-French Conve tion of 1901," in the" Carnhill Magazine "for June.

div.head: Why not Plant a Security.
div.p: Why not Plant a Security.

A young Scandinavian engineer had, by dint of hard work, patienc,e,and economy, accumulated a few thous- and dollars, with which he leased and equipped a small engineering works, in which he undertook all sorts of job work. He succeeded so well that within five years he was able to employ about fifty mechanics. Business flourished. He extended his works, and soon hada very considerable establishment. In the year 1895 he pro- cured a large Government contract, but the terms were such that he could only receive the first payment upon completion of a certain portion of the work. He soon found himself short of 'cash," and at once applied to his banker. The year 1895 was not a very favourable year for American trade, and the banks were unusually cautious in view of the recent panic of 1893. The banker naturally demanded security before making the loan, but all the young engineer had to offer was his factory and business. Needless to say these assets—although an absolutely essential part of a nation's wealth—did not come within the term" good banking security." He then applied to various brokers and financial firms, with the same result. At last he found the man who was willing to advance the neces- sary funds—for a consideration, the consideration be- ing, first, a judgment note, or bill of sale, and, second, interest at the rate of 50 per cent, per annum, payable quarterly, in advance! For two years he manfully fought this uphill battle, paying the usurer promptly the amount stipulated. Then he lost his health, next his business, then he died, and finally the sheriff took possession. and the money-lender got the proceeds of the sale. The total results were that the money-lender —a non-producer—made a good profit on his invest- ment, while the United States lost a wealth producer,a valuable citizen and a good industry i .—Arthur Kitson n London Opinion. " T.P." on Lord Curzon.

"T.P." in " M.A.P." says of Lord Curzon :—" In physical appearance, in bearing, in language, Lord Curzon reveals the man he is almost more clearly than any man I know. The fine height, the face with its well chiselled features, its aquiline and haughty nose its eyes, wide, large, prominent, open, daring, tho rich colouring of the complexion, are the proper outward of a man who is full of those qualities which make one a leader among men. It is all these things that account for what was certainly something of an obstacle in the early age of Lord Curzon's career. I will not repeat here the rhynie which has been quoted usque ad:nauseant against him. 'Whenever an ill-natured thing has been sad lof a man of real ability, there are always plenty of people who are ready to remember and to propagate it. If human nature were only as retentive in its memory of the kind and eulogistic things said of men as of the , malicious and the unjust, many historical verdicts would have to be reversed. Suffice it to say that, though Lord Curzon has undoubtedly that full self-confidence which is one of the necessary qualities of a leader of men and of men of action. I do not think that his self-estimate has ever been beyond his deserts ; and he has always appeared to me in private a very courteous and a "'very unpretentious man. If 1 were asked what was the first and main secret of Lord Curzon's extraordinary success, I should say that ha is above and before all things a politician. I have said it so often that I am almost ashamed of repeating it, but I think the curse of this country is that its politics are so much in the hands of amateurs. Men in England, and especially perhaps in the Conservative party, take their politics as more or less part of the usual round of pleasures of which their lives consist, just as they take hunting and shooting and the gaieties of the London season. Such, then, is the man who for the moment is a visitor to the shores of his native land. He will probably be soon among his own people again, and may be in the running for one of the high places in the government of his country. He may. be Foreign Secretary in a new Administration, he may even reach higher. At all events, he is among his own people once anin after five years of hard and strenuous exile,, and everybody will join in the welcome that is given to him. A wel- come of equal cordiality will be given to the beautiful and gracious daughter of America who is his consort and his help-meet, and who—belonging to that extra- ordinary race which is now dazzling the world—has proved that the child of a Republic may take her place —almost as of right—as the worthy companion of an exalted ruler.

div.head: Mr. Gladstone and Lady Politicians.
div.p: Mr. Gladstone and Lady Politicians.

In connection with the coming conference of lady Liberals, it is interesting to recall Mr. Gladstone's atti- tude toward the lady politician. In spite of the face that he paid Women the compliment of saying that at platform orators he feared they would ultimately eclipss the men, he never championed the cause of the lady politician, or sympathised with her views on the sub- ject of Woman's Rights, although he considered ladies valuable as canvassers. Perhaps he agreed with Dr. Johnson that" Nature has given women so much power that the law wisely elves them very little." Never- theless, in spite of his views on the subject, he was re- sponsible for the making of at least one ardent lady politician, Lady Sandhurst, who declared it was the inspiration of Mr. Gladstone's handshake after her maiden speech that made her take up politics, and traverse the country speaking in favour of his Irish policy.—Mrs. Hugh Adams in London Opinion.

div.head: Hermit Who was Jilted.
div.p: A Hermit Who was Jilted.

There seems to be no doubt that if the times were only a little more propitious we should have quite a number of hermits in our midst. One is continually hearing of them, and their numbers seem to increase rather than the reverse. One of the latest to be publicly noticed is a Mr. Mason, who lives at Great Canfield, in Essex, and who for over 13 years is said to have lived in complete seclusion. This resolve is said to have arisen out of a vow that be would never look upon a woman's face again, in consequence of having been jilted in a love affair. It would seem that male faces are also included, for with . the exception of a brother only two men have caught a glimpse of him during the time. The hermit's farm covers an acre of ground, and is surrounded by a very high and thick hedge, along the bottom of which barbed wire is stretched. On the outer side of the main fence is a ditch 10ft, deep and 12ft. wide, the earth being banked up so as to Torm a barricade 20ft. high, and on the top of this another thick hedge is planted. This was done twelve years ago by the hermit, the work being carried out at night. Inside the fence is a labyrinth of trees and undergrowth, among which barbed wire is stretched, and also a shed with a corrugated iron roof and a brick chimney at the side. Mason makes his living by bee- keeping. His hives are to be counted by dozens, while the honey is disposed of by his brother. Women as Commercial Travellers.

It has often occurred to me (says the writer of the "Employment Bureau" in this week's "Hearth and Home") that there is a fair opening for energetic, capable, and strong, women as commercial travellers; the modern woman likes travelling about, she is not. inflicted with an undue amount of shyness, and it con- siderable number of Englishwomen have thoroughly good business heads. Such being the case, it seems to me there is considerable scope for women who will at as agents for all kinds of goods specially adapted for women's needs and women's fancies. It is not, however, in England that thPre is any parti- cular demand for women in this line of business ; it is on the Continent that there is at present opening for both men and women as commercial agents, and in ninny ways, and for many articles, women are better equipped than men for this work. The lack of English commercial travellers in foreign countries is largely due to ignorance of foreign languages, which is more often found among men that among present day women. As a rule, girls who have hdd an ordinarily good educa- tion can very quickly pick up enough of a foreign lang- uage for conversational purposes. If such would enter a business house for a- couple of years, and become thoroughly Conversant with one branch of trade, they would be competent to undertake the work of com- mercial travellers abroad, provided, of course, they feel able to manage such matters as getting accommoda- tion at out-of-the way places,planning routes, travelling economically and comfortably. The openings for women in the future will probably lie in the direction of business; those who feel any capacity that way had better qualify themselves as thoroughly and as quickly as possible, for to-day, more than in any other age, the race is to the swift.

div.head: (Copyright.)
div.p: (Copyright.)
CHARLIE RACE-TIE-WATER
BY MAY CROMMELIN.
Author of "Queenie," "My Jewel of a Girl,' • "Dust before the Wind," "Dead Men's Dollars," "Goblin Gold," Sze.

The world is in such a hurry nowadays, because mortals have begun to understand how much of Interest may be crowded into life, that to save my readers' time in understanding the locality of this tale, will they please to glance at a map of Ireland. Look north, at the county of Down. On its eastern coast, facing Scotland, they will see the peninsula of the Ards, hugging the mainland so close that it seems on paper as if the "back-sea," as the inner Strangford lough is called, were more like an inland lake than salt water. Not so in reality.

To see with what force the tide pours like a mill- race through its narrow sea channel and rushes up and up for miles, past a green-topped flock of islands, is a grand sight. At each ebb miles of hard sands are left bare at the lough-head. There is a track across these from the Ards to the main- land, used by carts or riding-folk at low water. A white pillar on each shore marks the spot, on which a red flag is hoisted at safe times by a man living in a cabin hard by, for, when the tide is flowing, however far off the blue streak may appear, its calmest wavelets will yet, with each slow kiss, cover yards of crinkled sand. Woe, then, to any loitering traveller caught midway on the track! On a still summer day lie will be submerged with smiling swiftness; but in wintry weather, with a west wind, the waves will leap like rdcing horses, even right over the coast-road, drenching fields, trees, and hedges with showers of spray. Towards the wane of the last century old Lord Mount-Alexander sat with a gloomy brow, his lace ruffles reflected in the polished brown mirror of the dining-table. His granddaughter of seventeen, Leila, watched him with clear eyes, blue as the sash that girt her muslin gown. Sympathy with his mood seemed to restrain the smiles lurking in the corners of her sweet mouth from brimming over at the sallies of her brother, Charlie Alexander. The latter, a merry undergraduate, was trying, poor fool! to heighten the gaiety of the party. The fourth at table was the old lord's nephew, Sidney Forbes, a pale, refined-looking young man, who watched his uncle with a constant deference only broken by admiring glances at his cousin, Leila, of which the young girl appeared artlessly unconscious. Dessert was on the table, and when the last servant left the room Lord Mount-Alexander looked at his grandson, saying sharply: "Demme, sir, pray cease prattling! Can't you see we have more serious matters to think of than to hear of your schoolboy pranks ? " "I am sorry, grandfather, to have vexed you. Still, as I only returned this morning, pray excuse my good spirits on being at home again," replied Charlie, reddening to the roots of his brown hair. His good-humoured face was so contrite, and his tone so manly and frank that the old man's brow cleared. _

But Sidney Forbes interposed with quiet reproof. "Had you given yorr grandfather or myself some more of your cc mpany to-day, instead of loitering in the kennels and stables, you might have learnt what is on his mind."

"Pray scold me for that, Cousin Sid. 'Twas I who dragged Charlie off with me, feeling glad of a new playfellow," apologised Leila, with a voice like a robin's note cheering a dark day. Then, appealing eagerly yet modestly to the old lord, whose favourite she was: "Pray, sir, tell Charlie about these highwaymen, who have now twice robbed your servants when you sent money in their care. He does not know of your anxiety to send safely this third time, seeing how strange it is that anyone should have known of your intention before, when it was kept so secret. Oh, a real robber haunts the road, Charlie! He has stopped several carriages, and taken old Lady Fitzwarrenne's diamonds from her—a thin man iid'ng a black horse with a white blaze. Sometimes another man is with him, and both ;re masked." Pausing to draw breath after her haste to place her beloved brother on an equal position of information with the, others, Leila saw the two elder men smiling indulgently. Lord Mount- Alexander, who was known to dislike many words, made a sign that Sidney should end the tale. "Chatterbox! You have not left me much to add, seeing the matter is as dark as the work of these gentry," said Sidney gently. Then, deprecating Charlie's hot questions with a wave of his white scholar's hand, he recounted matters in the tone of a philosopher, who looked on money merely as a means to gain those things he really prized—power and fame, first in Parlia- ment, then in the Government. Though only twenty-eight, Sidney Forbes, after distinguishing himself at school and college, aimed at represent- ing the county of Down, in virtue of his uncle's influence; and indeed his gifts, studiousness and ambition, had won him not only the admiration of his family, but the awed respect of the rollicking squirearchy around The first robbery was when the last half-year's rent had been `sent up to the Belfast Bank, three months ago. The old agent, a family friend, who was conveying the sum in his carriage, had been cruelly beaten, as also his two servants, and he still kept his bed from the effects. A second time a large sum had been sent, still more secretly, for this was intended to assist Sidney's coming contest of.the county. But on the way to Downpatrick the groom sent in eharge of it—a young, strong man— was found shot dead, his pockets rifled, and his horse grazing half a mile away. "And that incident might have ended my dreams of a public life, but for my uncle's great generosity," said 'Forbes, with gratitude enlivening his pale but handsome face. "Ah, Charles, dear lad, you who never care a jot for the advantages of education, who accept as a birthright, should reflect how lucky you are in being heir to a tioble title and fortune with the certitude of being able to serve your country in the Upper House." "Egad! it may berpoor service unless he mends his idle ways," rapped out the old man testily. "Also, I've no intention of dying for a good many years yet, Master Charlie! There! there!" as young Alexander burst out defending himself warmly from any imputation of filial heartlessness, his blue. eyes sparkling. "You are a good boy enough, though careless. Now, the point is, that my old friend, Colonel Stuart, has to-day unexpectedly repaid me a loan made him last year, which I once more intend for Sidney's benefit. If it goes to this deuced highwayman no grand tour for you Charles. No, no, no protestations, Sidney! You two boys are wt Lome to my ready cash to advance your true into e;ts. But Charles will acknowledge that travellirg on the Continent is not indispensable • to the at grandi:e.nent of the family, while to help my dead sister's son is so, seeing we all expect you, my dear f.ll,‘w, to become Sir Sidney Forbes, 8.P., his Mai, s y's Fr:ine Minister! This was a long speech f corn' his lord- ship. He ended abruptly: 'Now, who the due is to convey this money safely to Sir Alan Maunab, near Lisburn? And how and when shall I send it?" "Send me; I'll start. by da)light. I'll ride 'em a race!" cried Charlie, his boyish face alight with eagerness. Leila gave a low cry of dismay. Hearing it the grandfather, who had smiled well-pleased on his Leir, changed his expression to a benevolent denial. Sidney Forbes, with a quiet air of manli- ness, spoke up: "Let me go, sir'. and to-night. There is no time to lose, Jest the matter leak out as strar—ely as before. What! Shall I, a grown man, t. 1 v this dear scatterbrain.? of ours to risk a broken h -ad for my good? No, Ch trlie, wait till your beard is grown. I hope, Uncle Mount, you do not look on me as a mere polit'cian, but 'also as a man of spirit. Poor I am in fortune, yet--" Sidney broke off in a, fit of coughing which lasted some moments. When lie withdrew the laced handkerchief he had put to his lips it, was stained slightly with -blood. His uncle had eyed him with affectionate anxiety, then said, with a tone of firm- ness which none of his family ever dared to question. "No, Sidney, I refuse absolutely. Your safety is as precious to me as that of either of these two orphans. My dear fellow, your cough is distressing. You should ride or walk more; you study too late at nights. By Jove! I'll send old Mulligan. I could lay my life on his honesty. Mulligan was the old family coachman, one of those devoted retainers for which Irish households used to be famous. Charlie began expostulations. Mulligan was stiff, heavy in the saddle. Suddenly he felt Leila's slipper pressing his foot to enjoin silence. His grandfather, with an impatient gesture, dis- missed these obections, pointedly inviting Sidney's advice. To his chagrin Charlie found himself over. looked, as the others settled that the old servan

should be despatched when the rest of the house- hold were retired to rest, so as not to arouse suspicion in the stables. r.ut when next the elders coolly discussed whicl) horse old Mulligan should ride, Charlie's heart fairly boiled with indignation. From childhood he had been brought up at the Castle, had ridden every horse in its stables since he was a boy ; at sixteen he was held to have the best seat out hunting in the Ards, while at college his judgment on a nag's points was law. And now, forsooth —since he had been absent a year at college and travelling on the little tour during vacation—his grandfather seemed infatuated with this interloper of a nephew. Aye, and Sidney, bookworm, pedant, prig, was actually recommending the old roan as a steady mount for Mulligan. Out he burst: "I noticed a far better animal in your stable to- day, sir—a black horse, in the box next the door. He looks as if he had a turn of speed— "Why, bless me, that is my steady slug, gently laughed the philosopher. "He is slightly lame, toc • his shoe pinches. No, no, dear lad; don't propose risking my election on him!" "Prll the bell for Mulligan, and don't interfere with your cousin's affairs," said Lord Mount- Alexander shortly to his grandson. As Charlie obeyed, his round face became expres- sionless, only he shut- his mouth like a vice. Instead of resenting himself, he stood by the fire, as if ready to leave, having no further interest in the matter. Leila threw him a blue glance, then with a pretty shiver, came to warm litrlf by his side, pretending to push him away fi oin the warmest fp it. • -Yet, she passed her arm roun I her brother's neck next, with a sudden hug, she whApered : "Stay!" Charlie started, then he gave her ear a reassur- ing pinch. Mulligan as a man of sixty and withered, yet on hearing what was asked of him, he cocked his head with a rakish air, and answered joyously: "I'm the boy for this job. Gimme the parcel. I'll be off at wanst. By six o'clock the morrow, me lard, Sir Alan Mac Nab will have your honour's money, or ould Mulligan will not be alive to drive yer coach any more." ("The moon only rises past midnight, uncle, and these road gentry are surely less likely to be abroad in the small hours than now. But you should know best," murmured Forbes deferentially, his brow wrinkled with anxiety. "Excuse my suggestions; but my future is at stake.") Lord Mount-Alexander reflected a few moments. Meantime, old Mulligan, giving a shrewd leer at Forbes, turned eagerly to the pair at the fireplace, as if seeking support. "Masther Charlie—" he began.

"Attend to my orders, sirr:",h," called out his master, in sudden anger. "Mr. Charles has no more to say than his sister in the matter. Here is the parcel. You will start at midnight precisely, and you will take the roan horse. You hear ? " "Aye, aye," answered the old servant soothingly. "I was only after thinking the nights is cowld. And the wild dyucks are plentiful, which, Masther Charlie might like till know." It was then nearly ten o'clock, at which hour Lord Mount-Alexander went to bed. Forbes took leave of his uncle, for he was in the habit of study- ing late, and was already preparing his electioneer- ing speeches. At the same time Charlie, with a big yawn, also approached, saying: "Good-night, grandfather; good-night, Leila. There is to be a meet of the harriers at Bangor to- morrow morning. I am thinking of going, so must be off early." "Well, at your age, I was an equal fool. Sidney will be the first man of intellect our family has produced," replied the old man. (One short year ago he would have' cheerily wished Charlie a good day's sport.) Towards half-past eleven, there came a gentle tapping at Charlie's door. Leila's voice whispered through the keyhole: "It's only me! Indeed, I must speak to you. Charlie, don't blow the candle out. I know you are up—" "What the dickens do you want? " The door was cautiously opened a little way. When Leila slipped in, she saw that her brother was fully dressed in dark riding-coat and top-boots, all his late evening finery doffed. "I knew it—you are going with Mulligan," cried the girl. "That's why I sat up. 0 dear Charlie, is it worth risking your life to gain a seat for our detestable cousin ? "

"No. But it is to secure the grand tour for my- self," grinned Charlie. Then tapping his pockets: "I've got my pistols, and [fancy I know how to use '.hem, though I am a' dear scatterbrains'! So you hate Sidney, eh? Yet, I saw him casting sheep's eyes all day, when he would come after us even to the stable-"

"He makes love to me for my money; but if I were penniless I would never take him," uttered Leila hotly. "And as to the stable, just because his new groom was there—Mulvaney, a sneak and blackguard, so Mulligan warned me—l would not tell you that my young thoroughbred mare is a splendid goer. Take her. Here is the key of her box. Yes, it never leaves me. And Mike Mulligan, my foster-brother, you know, has a second key. Oh, - tha:ntc Heaven you are home again! Grandfather seems bewitched, and only thinks of Sidney's politics, and talks of how to raise money by cutting trees, so that the county member may make a proper show in Parliament. He pooh-poohs these smuggler stories; while Sidney seems fooled in his turn by Mulvaney— Leila stopped short, half crying. Charlie uttered a long "Wh—ew! I heard to-day that the smug- glers were active again. So, plainly, you think Mulvaney is th'ck with them? That is why you keep this key? Silly I—they would not dare to steal from us." "No, But to borrow, at. nights. Listen, Charlie. Sidney believes his horse is slow, but Mulvaney knows the contrary. I myself have seen the poor beast lying down in his box some mornings, too tired to stir." "The devil! Then Mulvaney may be the traitor who warned this highwayman! But if Sidney guessed—why, the last money robbed was for his own election business." "'Twas the biter bit; but he is too pompous to believe a girl like me. Besides, Mulvaney is a kind of Mephistopheles to our philosopher Faust. Oh, t,he family scholar is too learned to hunt or shoot; but still he is not too fine a gentleman to scorn low village intrigues. But I'll say no more." As Leila stopped short, with heaving breast and flashing eyes, Charlie opened his eyes in amazement. Only to-night he thought his sister still a child! She went on hastily: "There! all this talk is delaying you; and you should start soon. How frightened I am for you! Yet, Mulvaney, if he is the culprit, has no time to pick that silly Sidney:s brains to-night or to warn Black Joe, as they call the highwayman." She was right. Without more words, Charlie tied a muffler round his th,o,,t, crammed his beaver low on his head, and with a hasty kiss to his sister went downstairs. Half-an-hour later, two 'riders were leaving the long sea-drive and emerging on to the high-road that followed, the shore. They were engaged in friendly dispute; for Mulligan, although proud of his Young master's company, was disinclined to hand over' the parcel, which "the ould lord" had confided to his express care. True, his horse was slow, and himself "no' that young. Still, divil a hair I care, for I'm just spoiling for a fight," he ended. They had not gone more than three miles, when Charlie remarked, in a low tone of surprise, both being careful to speak in muffled voices: "Your horse is tired or ill, surely! We are only beginning our journey, yet he does not care to trot. "Be jabers, I'll make him care," muttered old Mulligan, applying whip and spur. But to his great annoyance, these seemed to have no more effect than if his beast had been of wood. Slower and slower went the roan; yet he shewed signals of distress, breaking out in .sweat, and breathing heavily. At last, in spite of a flogging, he dropped to a walk. gad! he's been hocussed," muttered Charlie. tg Eh ? "Be the holy poker, I'm thinking that same," groaned the old servaat. "Now, is it that baste, Mulvaney ? For, if so, he knows I'm out this night—and why. But who in the .name of wonder tould him? " "Who, indeed?" echoed Charlie, stopping short in the shadow of a wood. His young face was set stern, and he was thinking harder than ever in his life before. Then suddenly he decided. :ot, must knowllg mare;/,--else why drug the and she is our “Hand the packet over Mulligan—quick. You ' roan. orneaentc. You heavy How is the tide?" "She's turned, she has! For any sake, boy. don't you thry it and be dhrownded ? Ochone—one! Quit it, and come home, Masther Charlie! " But even while thus appealing, Mulligan handed over the precious parcel, the habit of obedience being strong. The wood was on the right hand. A few yards ahead rose a landmark on the shore to left. This was an enormous, solitary boulder, called by the country-folk the Giant's Jackstone, large enough to shelter a cart and horse from sight. Past the

shadow of these the road ahead lay white fit the moonlight, with a low sea-wall on the one side and high hedge on the other. Nothing—no one was in sight. Charlie made up his mind. "Good-bye, Mulligan, I'm off!" And giving his eager mare her head he cantered into the moonlit space. Hardly had he done so when the sound of hoofs striking rock sounded behind, and a mounted man shot out from the shelter of the great Jacksl one, and, crossing a flat reef, entered the road where the sea-wall began. At the same time, he gate a shrill whistle. This was answered by the appearance of another rider ahead—a black apparition who stole silently out through an open gate in the hedge, which had hidden him from view. Charlie had turned in his saddle to look back, the next glance forward shewed the second adver- sary. This was a tall man on a black horse—Black Joe without a doubt. Both men were masked, and from both came the hoarse cry: "Stand, and deliver, or we'll shoot?! They were answered by a shout from poor Mulligan in the distance, who, no doubt, was vainly struggling to urge on his sick animal. Through Charlie's head flashed the thought: "Caught in a trap, two to one! Fight or run ? " He chose flight, and small blame to him. Coolly, as if unafraid, he cantered forward towards the black horseman, the barrel of whose pistol gleamed in the ,moonlight. Then, just before coming into range of fire, he wheeled his excited mare sideways, and with a grip of the knees that thrilled her to answering resolve, with a cut of the whip and a cheering cry he put her at the wall. Hooray! they were over! She pecked on the other side, for the beach was stony; but recovering herself gallantly, the frightened creature stretched out next moment in a mad gallop, it was all Charlie could do to guide her, but he dared not ride straight ahead across the desert of crinkled sands, for out there lay a quicksand. He must still hug the shore awhile, though at some distance. Therefore, if Black Joe chose to follow, the scoundrel had the advantage of a short cut. He did! Two pistol shots startled the night. Then, as Charlie looked back with a mocking laugh, it was echoed by another. Black Joe had leaped the wall after firing, and was riding to head Charlie to yards the dangerous spot. The latter set his jaw hard and scanned the wide sand-floor with keenest eyes. Not for nothing had he ridden by that shore since he could sit in a sad lie. Ahead there should soon be—by the living ji. go there was !—a crescent reef. On, on, Mavourneen ! Thud upon thud the great'black horse behind came thundering, and a muffled call reached Charlie's ears: "Stop, fool! You'll be swallowed up alive! Stop!" For the third time there came the report of a pistol. A ball hit the peak of Charlie's saddle, glancing off; but, terrified at the report, Mavourneen darted forward like a loosed arrow, shewing a pair of clean heels to the black horse. "Steady, lass. So then, Mavourneen Steady!" The crescent reef was passed. Then, with a strong pull, Charlie turned the mare's head towards the open ,sand, far, far across which, -low and dark in the moonlight, lay the opposite shore. Now he must steer to left of yonder grass-topped islet, between two more reefs. These passed, he would strike the true track, and it would be a race! Till then, .if Black Joe tried the sands to either side, he was a dead man.

The highwayman did not attempt it. Plainly he was astonished, but judged that where the mare went safe, he would follow. But, even as Charlie glanced back, he saw a flounder, a struggle. The black horse had slipped on the rocks and both were down. And at the same moment he became con- scious that his own pistol was grasped in his hand. A voice seemed to cry in his ears: "Now! Now! Kill him! Pull up and fire! He tried to shoot you!" Almost unconsciously Charlie held Ifavonrneen in, half-turned, cocking the trigger. Next instant the word Murderer! seemed whispered by another voice in his soul. Rousing himself with a feeling of shame he galloped on—on----- Before he had gone six lengths the black horse and his rider were up again and after him. "Forred! forred!" cried Charlie to the game lass he rode, and she cocked 123 r ears and made a fresh spurt. They had gone a mile in that wild gallop, when Charlie remembered the tide and looked leftwards. God! what was that sheen yonder? The tide! The tide! It was coming up! It was close! The land ahead was now clear to see, yet he could never gain it, even at this racing pace, and if Mavourneen held out—never before the terrible tide! And it he risked racing in front of the water right up to the lough head, there were quicksandt ahead, besides the fel r that the mare could nit keep up this killing p ice on the yielding sandt Yet it was the last chance. Charlie wheeled ant took a line at right angles to his former course, glanced at Black Joe, who had not caught him up, nor yet lost an inch since his fall. The highway- man wheeled more slightly, thus gaining ground with every stride. He yelled across the intervening waste: "Stand!" _

_ "The tide! The tide!" shouted Charlie: "Keep left for your life, man! 'Ware shifting sands!" For his practised eye saw between them a sandy space that seemed to shiver faintly. The next minute Black Joe, never swerving, was in it, was flounder- ing, his horse up to its fetlocks. Charlie, after that warning cry to his foe, lut,a not looked back. His whole mind, skill, were needed to save his own life, to urge on Mavourneen yet spare her strength for the last, when she must, perhaps; swim. Then a faint, despairing cry reached his ears: "Charlie I. Help! Heavens! whose was that familiar voice? With the instinct to save life he tried to pull in the Mare, although knowing it might be fatal to himself. Then he saw; understood! The black horse was plunging wildly in sand and water, his rider madly flogging. The tide was oA them! Even as Charlie watched, horror - stricken, long crawling wavelets lapped round Mavourneen's hoofs.

With a frightened whinny she bolted, taking the bit in her teeth—away, away on and on; racing before the tide. Each instant Charlie expected to be engulfed, like him behind. In the awful horror and dread fallen upon him he could only keep his saddle and knew no more, till at last came hard ground, the dark line of a hedge close before his straining eyes. Then a rise in the air, a fall down, down— When Charlie recovered consciousness next morn- ing, he was lying in a roadside cottage, with a bandaged head. He tried to speak, when kindly rough voices answered: "Aye! yer mare is safe. She's a grand yun! All the boys going to the fair this morning is afther calling ye Charlie-race-the-water! Man dear, but ould Mulligan raised the eountryside finely to thry and save ye. Yer grandfevther is down by the shore this minnit. For the other poor gentle- man• Mister Forbes, they call him—has been, found ! "

Found, indeed! with the remains of a black mask still hanging round his neck was Sidney Forbes, his face stiffened in an expression of agony! A. black horse was cast up, too, by the tide, with 3 white blaze of paint smeared on its forehead.

• • • . • • • • "My boy! my own dear boy! Thank God you are safe!" faltered old Lord Mount-Alexander, with tears in his stern eyes. "Let us bury this family disgrace, deep. Mulligan will be silent out of loyalty. Mulvaney has escaped. Any others who guess I will pay to hold their peace." Charlie drew the packet of money out with a shudder, saying feebly: "Use this—for him still.,
LTII3 END. 1

THE DUTY OF FREE TRADERS.

ON May 15th, 1903, Mr. Chamberlain first launched his proposals of what he describes as • " Fiscal Reform." His policy has been greatly modified in some directions and considerably extended in others. Originally started as a great Imperial scheme to unite the Empire by the institution of preferential tariffs, it developed into a proposal of general Protection in which the Empire had a small part. A year's campaign has sufficed to bring about many changes. For this and other reasons the time had come when re-consideration of the whole position and a re-statement of the case from Mr. Chamber- lain's point of view was necessary. This was given at the annual meeting of the same Association before which Mr. Chamberlain's scheme was originally placed. This meeting was held at Birmingham on May 12th. As he said It may b useful, twelve months later, to take stock of the result, to estimate the situation in which we find ourselves.

Reviewing the Situation. Jr Mr. Chamberlain is a pessimist about the future of British trade, he shewed himself very optimistic when speaking to his friends on May 12th of the " success " his proposals had achieved in the country. He argued that a question which has aroused so much interest can never die. He told us that he neither expected nor desired an early Success; on the contrary, he thinks any haste would be a great -r.vn we remember that a year ago we were told the Empire was in danger of falling into .disjointed atoms, this assurance of the needlessness of hurry is comforting. Mr. Chamberlain congratulated himself ihat he had captured or converted the Unionist party. Said he:
JalicrtTtrke.

The Unionist party almost unanimously in the House of Commons, even more unanimously in the country, is pledged at least to this: to endeavour to recover the power of retaliation, the loss of which far-seeing statesmen regretted fifty years ago, and the restoration of which has been desired by far-seeing statesmen since.

div.head: A- Terrible Person
div.p: A- Terrible Person

THEN he went on to tell us that the mere threat of what he would do if he got the chance had brought foreign nations to their senses! The late Colonial Secretary evidently thinks himself a very terrible person, whose mere word is sufficient to do all that is required to preserve our Colonies from the evil designs of foreign nations. Because certain German Jingo newspapers have forgotten to breathe out senseless threats against British Colonial trade, Mr. Chamberlain imagines he has influenced the German Government. One oan only hope foreign statesmen have a little more common sense, when they review the position of British politics, and do not take our Daily Mail as the mouthpiece of the nation.

Foreigners Frightened. THEN Mr. Chamberlain tells us he has Met certain unnamed and unknown foreign manu- facturers who are terribly upset at the prospect of his possible success' and who in such an event are coming over to Great Britain to set up their works here! This chatter about "people I have met" is really most uncon- vincing. Any globe-trotting Briton could tell far more exciting tales of the deep ways of the artful foreigner. Dumpers in despair.
WE were next told that as a result ofthe Tariff Reform agitation there had been a "noticeable diminution of dumping." The reasons given for this are most entertaining, and must be given in full:

That is attributed to the fact that our ingenious and energetic competitors thought it prudent to stop their hands for a while, and to send their surplus goods in other directions rather than irritate a controversy which already they would desire to put to rest.

This shews Mr. Chamberlain has simple and childlike ideas about business which were supposed to be somewhat foreign to his general character. He seems to think foreigners shoot their goods upon our shores without being asked, and that no British importer is in any way responsible! It is sad to have to relate that as long as British merchants can buy " dumped " goods from the foreigner cheaper than from anybody else they are rot likely to be disturbed by Mr. Chamberlain or his Tariff Reform League. But alas! in this matter Mr. Chamberlain is wounded in the house of his friends, for at the very time he was speaking came the message that 5,000 ions of Canadian bounty-fed billets are on their way to this country. If our Colonial brethren are proof against Mr. Chamberrain's threats, how can he hope to impress the foreigner?

div.head: Defeated or Defiant?
div.p: Defeated or Defiant?

STILL, Mr. Chamberlain is so elated with his " success " that he imagines the country is anxious to express its gratitude and confidence in him! If the people of this country wore only given the chance to express an opinion upJn his scheme and his scheme alone, he says:
Honestly I believe that by a g ea majority they would vote in favour of the change.

Unfortunately, there are so many other subjects which interfere with a straight vote. There is the Education Act, with which people do not agree, and with whom Mr, Chamberlain sympathises. There is Chines.° Labour, which may be good or had. Then there is the Licensing Bill, which is causing so much trouble just now. All these things, according to Mr. Chamberlain, are so many weights which drag down those Tariff Reform candi- dates who otherwise would be victorious at every election. Tariff Reform, according to Mr. Chamberlain, instead of being a handicap to Unionist candidates, has been the one subject that has saved them from utter disaster, it is, in his opinion, the one asset of the Unionist party, and success has !followed. those candidates who, in the parlance of the hour, are "whole-hoggers "

those candidates who had a little courage, who dared to call their souls their 'own, who had supported with all their might, whole-heartedly, the policy in which they believed, and who had earned, and deserved to earn, the result of their courage.
It is refreshing to have Mr. Chamberlain's candid opinion about gentlemen who are on the fence over this question. Said he:
IT IS NOT GOOD POLICY-TO SAY NOTHING AT ALL ABOUT MORALITY-TO SIT UPON THE FENCE.
Thus we see that, so far from admitting he has been *defeated, Mr. Chamberlain claims he is winning all along the line. In his closing words he told his Birmingham friends :

I know that liirmingliam.has sometimes been a little ahead of the country. The country has always come up to it in time, ana now I rely on you to help me to carry forward this beneficent rt form, which will be the crowning get and glory of our polities] associlt ion.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

LOCAL WEDDING.—The marriage was solemnized at St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey, of Mr. William Light - foot, third son of Captain Lightfoot, of Warrington- road, Penketh, and Miss Ruth Matthews, second daughter of Mr. Charles Matthews, also of Penketh. The Vicar, the Rev. .T. R. Jones. officiated. The contractingparties are well known in the neighbourhood, and a large con- gregation witnessed the ceremony. The bride was becomingly attired, and was given away by her father. The bridesmaids were Miss Emily Matthews (sister of the bride) and Miss Alice Lightfoot(sister of the bride- groom). Mr. John Tucker discharged the duties of best man. Numerous presents were received.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR

Councillor Maginn and the Lowest Tender. Sir,—The workers are indebted to the Amalgamated Society of Cabinet Makers for taking thelinitiative as an organized body—in protesting against Councillor Maginn's motion re the accepting of the lowest tender, which willlbe sub mittedf or discussion at the forthcoming Council meeting. I must express Fay surprise that the proposal of the representative of St. John's Ward has not been received with the emphatic and spirited con- demnation it justly deserves. And I say for one branch out of the numerous sections of organized labour in this industrial centre to be standing alone in dee nouncing the introduction of a principle in I.famieipiel Government that has clearly for its object the perpetuation of a system of demoralizinp, and soulless competition does not reftezt extraordiunay credit on the perception of the Titans of labor, on local management. I maintain it is the duty ori eters,- worker to make hie voice heard—loud enough to reach the Council Chamber—in protest against this. obnoxious proposal which is virtually an incentive too.n anarehistic and barbarous industrial scramble for existence. To quote Rathbone Grez, "Competititm dlitts our markets, enables the rich to take: advantage of the necessity of the poor, makes each, man snatch the bread out of his neighbour's mouth" converts a nation of brethren into a mass of hostile isolated units and finally involves capitalists and labottrers in one common ruin." Ponder well over these few words of Rathbone Greg. We are all employers of labour, we are nll shareholders iu the great concern of Warrington, Limited. It is essential if we desire to retain our good name of "model employers "to insist en our unpaid directors 'the oeces- sity of fair and honourable conditions, either in the employmentof labonr or the accepting of contractors. Warrington Limited is not run by a few interested financiers for personal gain and proit, but" by the veople for the people:" This may be objected to as inaccurate. Then if not, why not? If our Board of Management itecepts this motion they will mos decidedly be binding us to tutpleasant,cruel and awkward conditions, and as Mr. Edgar points out in a local con- temporary, will have a nattnral tendency to lower the standard of !lain.." of the working classes. And let as recollect in discassine the probable effect of this grotesque proposal that there are employers with souls mid consciences who are anxions to act as generous and liberal to their empioyees as our system of individualism will permit. Then in the name of that atom of Christianity we still priers) ourselves in posssessing,let us as acommanity,participators in a great, business concern, direct our efforts in dereloping condi- tions that wilt broaden the intellectuality and give -reasonable opportunities for man to display the best side of his nature. I perceive the motion is so worded as to give local contractors rale advantage in the com- petition, for it goes on to.say "to accept the lowest 'tender, except only in cases where any person tendering carries on business within the bororgh and which the committee for special reasons may consider it not sdvisable to accept the lowest tender." The proposer of the motion, the egregieres Councillor Maginn, declared repeatedly last.:(9cto bar inlanguageof brill ianteloquence that would make our modern cioeros look .small, his anxious desire to serve the working classes if returned to the Council Chamber. Now then we come to the 'testing of this'profession of -sympathy. Why net add to the motion 'tkat when a local tender is accepted andtemployment of labour entailed that it be executed" within the thorough" and the standard rate of wages recognised. We do not want cheap clap-trap and false economy. Let our cceancillars of St. John's Ward or any other ward be streightforward and practi- cal. To use the exact words of Councillor Magiim in the course of a debate at the last meeting of the Cotencil 4' it is wiser to takethe bull by t.he horns and to-spend rather than adopt .a niggardly economy:" 'apologize for occupying so much a your vrEuable space.— Yours, etc.,
A GENERAL TABOURER.

We could exhibit them in turns every Saturdayafternoon on some of our largest football fields, and there would be a record gate to see the show. The operatives of Lancashire would gladly provide all the rotten eggs and interesting missiles that would be required to pelt with,and thousands of willing hands would have a shie at them. It would be a drastic remedy, but it would be effectual. It would be fine fun for some of us, but it would be death to cotton corners and gambling. If the rogues came out .of the pillory alive they would never face the music again. But if you are going to adopt my suggestion you must not let the rich rascals off by paying fines. You must make no distinction between rich thieves and poor ones. on must bring home this drastic punishment to every one of them. But let us start with the big sinners first.

VOLUNTEER HORSE RACES. A Bank Holiday Attraction at Wilderspool. Warrington had a unique and decidedly interesting Whit Monday attraction in the regimental horse races promoted by the local Volunteer Battalion. Hitherto the contests have taken place during the annual encamp- ment, but it was felt that the townspeople would be glad of the opportunity of witnessing expert riding by the members of the Mounted Infantry Company which is an efficient and nerd working seztion of the battalion. Besides, there were worthy objects to which the pro- ceeds could be devoted. The Volunteer quarters are undergoing extension at a cost of about £3,000 and increased funds would be acceptable to help on the work of the Mounted Infantry Company. One of the large fields off Wilderspool Causeway made an admirable racecourse, and the promoters went to no little expense in erecting stands for the accommodation of spectators. It was unfortunate that the weather conditions were not more favourable. Rain fell for several hours to the discomfort of those spectators who were not under coder. There was lan attendance of between 2,000 and 3,000, and a capital afternoon's sport was witnessed. A programme of seven events was gone through, the competitors numbering about fifty. Thanks to the excellent arrangements, the proceedings passed off without a hitch, and there were no serious accidents. Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall were among the spectators on the grand stand, and Lady Greenall distributed the prizes after each race until five o'clock when she had to leave to catch a train en route for Brussels, wkere Sir Gilbert had arranged to judge at a horse show. The other awards were distributed by Mrs. Edelsten, wife of Lieut.-Col. J. A. Edelsten com- manding the Ist V.B. Prince of Wales's Volunteers (South Lancashire Regiment). The officers present, in addition to Col. Edelsten, were Col. Ridgway, V.D. (lately commanding the corps), Col. Buckton, Majors J. D. Fairclough, B. Fairclough, and F. M. Appleton,Capt. and Adjutant A. F. Bundock, Captains G. R. Crosfield, R. Smith, H. G. Roberts, C. L. Williamson,P. N. Avery, and C. F. Cary, and Limits. E. Ridgway, H. Owen, R. McM. Roberts,E. A. Connor, and A. B. Layton, Quarter- Master and Captain "A. F. G. Potter, Surgeon-Captain Curtis,Acting-Chaplain W.Bracecamp,andSergeant-Major Rawlinson. The duties of stewards were discharged by' Edelsten, Majors B. Fairclough and F. M. Appleton, Captains Bundock, Crosfield, Haslam, and Lieut. E. Ridgway. The other officials wele :1 president of the Race Committee, Capt. Avery ; hon. treasurer, Major J. D. Fairclough • clerk of the course, Capt. R. Smith • starter, Surgeon-Captain W. Curtis ;clerk of the scales, Smith; HG. Roberts. Capt. Bundock acted as judge. Most of the work of making arrangements devolved upon Captain Avery and Colour-Sergeant Bullen to whom special praise is due. During the afternoon selections were rendered in creditable style by the.
