div.head: Latchford Wesleyan Church Bible Class.
div.p: Latchford Wesleyan Church Bible Class.

On Sunday an open meeting of this class was held and a good congregation assembled. The address was given by Mrs. Moores, of Warrington. The soloist was Miss B. Carriage,who sang with much feeling " He wipes the tear from every eye" and "Jesus lover of my soul." The chairman was Mr. W. Beswick, and the organist Mr. C. Wood.

div.head: Sharp-street Sunday School Anniversary.
div.p: Sharp-street Sunday School Anniversary.

The anniversary of the above place of worship was held on Sunday. The preacher morning and evening wasithe Rev. J. Davies, of Grappenhall. The children and choir, who rendered special hymns, were most ably conducted by Mr. Jones. Mr. Whitley, of Stockton Heath, conducted a children's service in the afternoon, There were good congregations at each service. The total receipts for the day amounted to .28.

div.head: Rev. F. -G. West In Natal.
div.p: The Rev. F. -G. West In Natal.

Interesting accounts are received of the success with which the Rev. F. G. West, who visited Warrington re- peatedly in connection with the Baptist Churches and Wycliffe P.S.A. Society, is meeting in his new position as Baptist ministerat Maritzburg, Natal. According to a character sketch which lately appeared in the" Natal Mercury," the church was rarely more than half-filled up to Mr. West's advent :—Scarcely a month had passed before the rev, gentleman's force of character made itself felt. Crowds followed him. The church was invariably filled to an uncomfortable degree, and from his first appearance until to-day he has never looked back. The largest building in the city is not too large for the, crowds which follow him, and his advent has given an undoubted Slip to religious work wherever carried on. "Lazy" churches are being exer- cised la a way that they have never experienced before, and social and moral questions as touched by Mr. West derive fresh interest and importance. Sister Churches, which are dying of smug respectability or a sordid' materialisnr, may well pause and wonder at the result of nine months' work as achieved by this stranger, who, without the adventitious aids of oratory or great intellectual qualities, has made himself a power in the community.

Baptist Church Sunday School Anniversary. The Sunday school anniversary services were held on Sundayand the day was beyond doubt the most success- ful in the history of the church. There was a good con- gregation at the morning service when the Rev. H. Dunnico conducted the service. The choir gave the , anthem "How amiable are Thy tabernacles ' and the children sang a hymn. In the afternoon a musical ser- vice was held in the Parr Hall when there was a fairly large congregation. Alderman Bennett was prevented from presiding by illness and wrote expressing his re- gret, and speaking highly of Mr. Dunmco's work. In the evening the hall was crowded long before the time for commencing and in the opinion of the hall keeper there was a record attendance for the Parr Hall, many being turned away. The pastor again conducted the ser- vice, being assisted by the Rev. Thomas Fenton. The choir gave the anthems" Come unto me " and " Sun of my soul." The collections for the day amounted to £55 is. ld.—the highest sum yet raised at these anni- versary services. The choir, under the able leadership of Mr. T. Brough acquitted themselves in an able manner and won general piaise. Mr. Albert Trow pre- sided at the organ.

div.head: Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Mission.
div.p: Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Mission.

For some time past the workers- in connection with this place of worship have been putting forth every effort to raise the necessary funds to erect a more worthy and substantial building than the mission in which they now worship. With a view to helping the new Building Fund the single young mdn promoted a tea and social ',which took place on Whit Mon- day. The young men took entire charge of the arrangements. and carried the function through in a manner which did them credit. After tea games were indulged in, interspersed with one or two songs, a humorous sketch, a hat-trimming competition for men, and last, but in nowise least, a presentation on, behalf of the Young Men's Sunday School Class to Mr. Thoma 4 Ellison, who was married some weeks ago.— Mr. J. Barlow, who made the presentation, which took the form of a writing desk, said he hoped that the recipient, as well as the younger members of the family, would do their best to maintain the honour which had been attached to the name of Ellison ever since the Mission started.—Mr. Ellison fittingly responded, and expressed his sincere thanks to the donors of the hand- some gift.—The proceeds of the party amounted to £5 4s. 2d.

div.head: GRAPPEN HALL
div.p: GRAPPEN HALL

THE CRICKET CLUB.—The Ist eleven had for their opponents High Legh, at High Legh. The home play- ers won the spin of the coin and took first knock, in cold wet and miserable weather. The first two batsmen, Gorton and Lister settled down and between them com- piled 52 ; the former claiming 32, while the latter had 22 to his credit. Surridge and Blackburn came next in point of numbers with 12 each. High Leeh's total was 101. For the visitors Hallows bowled most effectively, 5 wickets for 33 runs, Carter coming secolki with 3 for 22. Grappen- hall's innings realised 90 for nine wickets. The chief contributors were Banks 20, England 14, and Warburton 13. The 2nd eleven at home, were defeated by Cronton. BANK HOLIDAY FIXTURES. The senior eleven played the annual fixture at Ashton Heyes. This is a day match and is very popular with the members. The Ashton eleven took the first innings making 48,Haycroft 14, and Nixon 12. Grappenhall replied with 89 Carter 29 Evans 14,Banks 12 and Ellis 10. The second innings brought forth 74 for 9 wickets when the homesters closed. Nixon again played a capital game and was responsible for 35, not out, with 33 to get and twenty-five in which to do it. Grappenhall commenced their second attempt and at call of time had put together 20 for the loss of no wicket. For the winners Carter and Warburton bowled well. The welther, beautiful when the match began proved rather fickle, but although rain did fall the match was not interfered with. The 2nd are in a losing vein and came back from Arley again on the wrong side.

div.head: STONTON HEATH,
div.p: STONTON HEATH,

ADVENTURE OF A. STOCKTJN HEATH GENTLF.MAN.— Among the fortunate or unfortunate pisiengers on boa rd the Isle of Mtn steamer Queen Victoria which on her return journey from the Island on Thursday afternoon broke one of her shafts and was, therefore, unable to proceed without assistance, was Mr. Thomas Williams, the well-known builder and parish councillor, of White- field-road, Stockton Heath. It appears that the steamer 'left Douglas at 4 o'clock and was expected to reach Liverpool before 7.30, but as before stated broke down owing to an accident to her machinery. Mr. Williams' opinion of the cause of the accident is" that those in command of the steamer were trying to break the record." This was to some extent accomplished as in- stead of arriving at Liverpool at about 7.15 in the even- ing she arrived at 5 o'clock the next morning. None of the passengers were any th 3 worse apparently for their unexpectedly long sea journey, and Walsh like made the best of the circumstances andalso of the provisions on board.

DROWNING CASE.—Mr. J. H. Fisher, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the London Bridge Inn, Stockton Heath, yesterday afternoon, touching the death of Joseph Bradshaw, a boatman, whose body was recovered from the Bridgewater Canal on Thursday.—The evi- dence showed that deceased and Walter Forster were employed on the narrow boats" Java " and "Japan," belonging to the Salt Union Company, Limited. They left Runcorn a week last Thursday and at 10 p.m.arrived at Stockton Heath where they tied the boats up. Forster went to bed, but deceased went ashore, returning about an hour later. He knocked Forster up, and after seeing deceased standing on the boat, Forster went to bed again. That was the last he saw of deceased until the body was recovered from the canal.—There was no evidence to show how deceased came by his death, and a verdict of "Found dead" Was returned.

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RESE,:ZVED.]
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RESE,:ZVED.]
SOCIAL SERMONET TES FOR WORKING MEN.
BY JOHN TAYLOR. Author of "Search Lights on Land, Labour and. Social Problems." THE TRICKS OF THE MEDIEVAL TRADER.

"The control of the medieval markets was under- taken by the Corporations to prevent frauds and adulteration of goods, and to keep prices at a natural level, and to regulate the cost of manufactured articles. The price of provisions was a subject of much regula- tion, but our forefathers were not very successful in carrying out their laudable schemes."—Giesnrs "INDUSTRIAL HISTORY OP ENGLAND." Human nature is much the same in all ages, and wher- ever you provide a public market place for the conveni- ence of honest producers and consumers, you will attract many crafty rogues, who hope to plunder both parties. The retail rogue will jerrymander your weights and measures, and pilfer and steal only articles of trifling value. But your wholesale thief, who has plenty of money, and some knowledge, will corner the mirket, and buy up all the supplies. And when he has created an artificial famine he will sell out at famine prices, and pocket his plunder joyfully. The cotton trade of Lancashire has suffered severely from the depredations of a gang of wealthy and un- scrupulous rascals, who neither use cotton themselves or let anybody else use it, unless they are willing to pay a ruinous toll to them. The men of this generation are familiar enough with "cotton corners," and "gam- bling in futures,' and "wheat monopolies," and "com- bines" to xi.'' the market and put artificial prices on everything. And when they pour their complaints into my ears they regard these rascally tricks as modern inventions of the devil, that had never been heard .of before.
1.-THE MEDIEVAL TRADERS KNEW HOW ITO
CAPTURE THE MARKETS.

You can take it from me that they knew a thing or two about "corners "and "combines," and" monopolies," but they did not call them by these names. They talked about "forestalling," and regrating," and "in- grossing," and these three old English words sound so strange to modern ears that I had better explain and illustrate their meaning. _ _

"Forestalling" was always regarded as an offence against public trade. An old Act of Parliament, passed in the reign of Edward VI., defines it as "the buy-ing,or contracting for any cattle, merchandise, or victual coming in the way of the market, or dissuading persons from buying their goods or provisions there, or per- suading them to enhance the price when there; any of which practices make the market dearer to the fair trader.' _

Regrating is described by the same statute as." the buying of corn, or other dead victual, in any market, and selling it again within the same market or within four miles of the place. For this also enhances the price of the provisions, as every successive seller must have a successive profit." " Ingrossing " means "the getting into one's possession, or buyingup large quantities of corn, or dead victuals of any kind, with intent to sell them again." This must beinjurious to the pablic, by putting it in the power of one or two rich men to raise the price of provisions at their own discretion. _ _ _

- Now I want you to observe that all these three offences are attacks on our food supplies, and on the necessaries of life ; and our medieval kings and Parlia- ments did not show much mercy to the food-gamblers and market-riggers of those days. They treated them as rogues and vagabonds, to be flogged, and fined, and pilloried, and imprisoned. They confiscated their stock-in-trade, and then handed them over to the tender mercies of;the mob,who treated them as roughly as a modern " welsher " is treated on the racecourse.
IL-MARKETS WERE ESTABLISHED TO GIVE EVERY BUYER AND SELLER EQUALITY OF OPPORTUNITY.

Our earliest trading laws seem to have been designed to give special protection to the ignorant, helpless clown, who had not will enough to look after himself. The authorities did most of his thinking for him, and if he had any brains at all he had not many opportunities of using them. Our market towns in those days were few and far between, and we had some of the vilest roads in the world, so the people of England did not spend much time in shopping. So our ancient fairs and markets were a very great convenience. They were usually held in the churchyard on a Sunday, or some other popular saint's-day. The people would g to an early service at church in the morning, and as soon as that was over the parson or the constable would cause the church bell to be rung, and declare the fair to be open to all COMM.
The authorities did not believe in secret buying and selling, and as a little money had to go a long way they tried hard to keep prices at a " natural level." . _ . _ _ . .

The "Assize Of - Bread and Ale "fixed the market price of these commodities every year, and it also fixed the rate of wages. If the price of food went up. and wages did not rise in proportion, there would be ructions and riots everywhere. So the authorities kept a sharp eye on every rogue who tried to send up the in to the of food by unfair methods. If a man came the market and spread false rumours to.create a panic and frighten men, they laid him by the heels very promptly. If a man attempted to buy or sell in the market before the appointed hour they promptly chucked him out, and confiscated his goods, and if he were a wise man he would take to his heels lest a worse fate befel him. If he bouglit anything in the market, and sold the same thing again in the same market, he was guilty of "forestalling," and he was punished by fines or imprisonment, or something worse. The manorial lords and the Corporations, who con- trolled these fairs and markets, were held responsible to the King for their good governmentand orderly manage- ment, and if any riots or disorder occurred they ran the risk of losingall their rights and privileges, and their charter would be taken from them. These public markets were established to bring the producerand the consumer into personal contact with each other, and to enable them to buy and sell freely at "natural level" prices. But there were "middlemen" and " brokers "and "gamblers" in those days, who objected to this arrange- ment, and wanted to know where they came in. They were neither producers nor consumers and according to the ethics of the times, they had no business in the market at all. But they had wit enough to know that by selling what they had not got, and buying what they did not need, And cornering the market, 'they might fleece everybody all round, and grow rich by methods that were little bettor than thieving. It is amusing to read what curious rules they made to keep prices down.and?,to give equality of opportunity to eve:ybody. If a carpenter bought more timber than he required because it was cheap, and inthe hope of sell- ing what he did not need at a profit, they accused him of forestalling, and they compelled him to sell it to any member of his gild at the same price he gave for it. If he refused to part with it on these tern* and could not use it himself, they confiscated his stock, and fined him, or gave him a treat in the pillory. It is highly edifying and suggestive to read witit elaborate preparations were made before every fair day for dealing with the social parasites who came there to prey on the legitimate traders. The authorities who controlled the fair had to fix the hours at which trading should begin and end. They had to see that all business was transacted during those hours, and that everythingishould be bought and sold publicly, in the open market, to give every citizen an equal chance. They had to provide competent inspectors of weights and measures, and supply.a number of capable " chuckers- out "to maintain order in the fair. And they had to set up a pillory, or a whipping post, or the stocks, or a ducking stool, for the punishment of offenders.__
ILL-THE PENALTIES FOR RIGGING THE MARKET WERE MANY AND VARIED.

•If fines were imposed, or if goods were confiscated all the plunder went to the Corporations, or manorial lords, who owned the fair or the market. So it was not to their interest to put any offender in the pillory or the stocks if they could squeeze any money out of him. It was no profit to them to flog and torture any offender, and if he could raise money enough to pay a fine he could save his skin and enrich them. This system of inflicting penalties on wrongdoers opened the door for all kinds of abuse. It gave us one law for the rich and another for the poor, and it taught bad men that they had better be wholesale thieves than small offenders. _ _ _ _

-- One enterprising gambler, who was neither a brick- maker nor a builder, made a corner in bricks, and he was fined £2O. which was a big sum of money in those days, and his bricks were confiscated. A butcher bought an ox. at a fair, and instead of turning it into beef he sold it again alive in the same fair, and was fined twice the value of the beast. Those offenders who could not afford to pay the fines had a rough time of it. For a first attempt at fore- stalling, the usual punishment was a fine of £lO, or imprisonment for twenty days on bread and water. For a second offence it was a fine of MO, or the pillory. For a third offence it was a fine of £4O, or the pillory, and the cutting off of one ear, and the loss of all civil rights and privileges. These punishments were terribly severe to the Door rascal who had no money. Twenty days in a medieval dungeon, with nothing to live on but stale crusts and cold water, is no equivalent for a fine of ten pounds, as it is outrageously unfair to let any rove escape the pillory who richly deserves it because he can pay a fine of twenty pounds. I should like to see the pillory set up again as a special treat for our cotton gamblers. It consists of two stout pieces of wood, firmly joined together, in the form of a cross. The top piece has three holes in it, that will hold the offender's head and hands. The bottom piece is made fast to the ground, and the victim has to stand for an hour or two in some public place, while the people play " Aunt Sally' with him. If we could cap-

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

An even draw was the result of Warrington's engagement with St. Helens on Saturday. Owing to the rain the start was delayed until nearly four o'clock and there was only a very small attendance of specta- tors. Warrington went in first and made a bad beginning, two wickets being down before a single run was scored. When W. H. Podnaore and E. Coke became associated, matters soon assumed a more encouraging aspect. The remaining batsmen all did well, and when 147 had been compiled for the loss of 6 wickets, the closure was applied. The visitors had responded with 76, with only' two wickets down,when stumps were drawn.

The best batting display was given by G-. H. Übsdell who knocked up 45 and carried out his bat. At first he played cautiously and hit many singles,but warming to the work, he gave bowlers and fielders a lively time. The Warrington captain, E. A. Connor, was in good form and hit out with his usual freedom. -At 20 he was caught by Wood from Urmson's delivery. W. Richardson, a promising recruit from the second eleven, placed 21 (not out) to his credit and W. H. Podmore was respon- sible for an excellent 17. B. Coke, who made first appearance in the eleven, batted in fine style and scored 10.

St. Helens had two reliable batsmen jh W. H. Ward and R. N. Turner who made a capital stand and had put together 33 and 24 respectively when play ceased. It was unfortunate that the time at/ the disposal of the cricketers was so limited, as otherwise the match would no doubt have been interesting and well- contested.

Warrington second team achieved a splendid victory at St.:Helens by a majority of 63. E. Pierpoint ran up the highes score of 25 for the victors, whilst on the St Helens sVe T. Cunliffe compiled 50. After his dis- missal the team soon collapsed, and Warrington had no difficulty in winning handsomely. Thewlis bowled with great effect and captured eight wickets for 24 runs, whilst Barber secured two for five.

After a lapse of several years, Warrington renewed their aquaintance with the Preston eleven on Thurs- day. The home organization was at full strength and included several players who have at various periods represented the County Palatine, whilst C. Wood of Broughton fame, is regarded as one of the most accomplished batsmen in club cricket. There were several absentees on the Warrihgton side, :and the absence of G. H. Üb3dell certainly weakened the attack. Before the Preston eleven had completed their innings, rain fell so heavily that the match had to be abandoned. The total stood at 209 for 9 wickets, C. Wood having knocked up 103 not out. His chief hits were eleven fours, ,eight threes. Lynes took 5 wickets for, 80, and Connor 4 for 39.

Sankey Wire Mills tried conclusions with Irlam C.W.S., the game ending in a draw. Irlam declared their innings after scoring 100 for the loss of five wickets, and Sankey had compiled 37 for four wickets when the time limit was reached. Etchells and Holmes batted well for the home team, Clarke (17) being the top scorer for the Wire Mills.

Stream' and Appleton defeated Lymm by the small margin of 4, thanks to the bowling of J. Ellison and J. R. Moorfield. On Monday the eleven did not fare well in their full day's engagement with Moore and Daresbury. On the first innings their opponents had the substantial majority of 61, but the issue of the second test was left undecided. Moore compiled 55 and Appleton had knocked up 49 for the loss of 9 wickets when the game closed.

There have been great doings at Penketh this week end. Sankey juniors visited the village determined to vanquish the Penketh Junior organization. They appear to have reached the height of their ambition, for we read that "the match resulted in an easy victory for the visitors by 146 runs." Foster was the hero of the day for he scored 100 not out and captured five wickets for 6 runs.

Grappenhall drew with High Legh,but the odds are that had time allowed they would have at any rate ended even with their opponents. High Legb.'s innings realized 104, to which R. H. Gorton contributed 30, and Grappenhall compiled 90 for the loss of 9 wickets. W. Banks,(2o) was the highest scorer for Grappenhall.

Penketh had no difficulty in disposing of Crostleld's who could make no headway against the bowling of Hobson and Shoobridge. Hobson captured five wic- kets for 51 runs. and Stoobridge was responsible for five at the extremely low lost of 4 runs.

Walker's Brewery met Winnington Park2nd and there is little doubt that had time permitted they would have achieved an easy victory. H. Cook gave a brilliant batting display, and carried out his bat after knocking up 125. His chief bats included twenty dfour fours. Tillino• and Ifiln:,•r did (Too work with the ball.

Cp.eshire Lines Engineers entertained St. FfelensSt. Thomas' and administered &feat to the extent of 17 runs. Riley's 20 was the top score for the engineers, none of the Saints making double figures. Jordan and Duckworth shared the bowling for the Cheshire Lines and succeeded in keeping the scores low.

Through SOMS reason or other—perhaps bad weather—Fairfield could only muster seven players against St. Paul's, but after some discussion they decided with this small number to play. Fairfield batted first, and owing to a very good and timely stand made by Messrs. It. Price and E. S. Haigh compiled the total of 72 runs. St. Paul's on going to the wicket were not equal to the occasion. The only member of their team who did himself justice was J. Ward, who made 22 runs, and the total score reached only 44 runs. Fairfield are to be congratulated on iheir plucky fight, and also on the fact that this is their fourth match and their fourth win. To-day they play Sankey Wire Mills 2nd at home.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

The pleasantly-situated bowling-green attached to the King and Queen was again thronged with enthusiasts on Saturday, when the first round of the popular works competition was continued. For the third time, a team which had entered for the contest failed to put in an appearance. On this occasion the missing bowlers were connected with Tinsley's Tannery, and consequently the team which should have opposed them—Fletcher Russell's—had a walk over. It would be well for all entrants to bear in mind that not a little inconvenienc is caused when they fail to fulfil their engagement. Teams are always notified of the time at which the matches commence, and if the bowlers down to play at 2.30 do not appear, the competition is at a stand- still for a considerable time. Entrants who cannot possibly take part might at any rate give the secretary a few days' notice of their intention.

There was an interesting match between Pearson and Knowles and Rylands No. 2. Each team fancied their chances, and the forgemen surprised their oppments by winning by 55 points. The victorious team is a fine organization, and includes some of the best players in Warrington. Mr. George Ball, jun., a well-known Lancashire county player, is the captain.

The first game between J. Worsley and F. Wood. was a very close affair. Worsley is a player of repute and was expected to win somewhat easily. Woods, created a surprise, and showed such good form that he was only beaten by a single point. George Ball made short work of his opponent, James Armstrong, and came out victorious by 15 points to 5. The con- test between Jas. Hardman and J. Warburton was extremely well fought, the first named winning by one point.

Of the twelve games; Pearson and Knowles won eightL Their chances for the final are iegarded as second to none, as last year they were within an ace of carrying off the trophy. In the deciding encounter London and North Western Railway triumphed. The forgemen have a particularly strong team this season and will take a great deal of beating.
Crosfield's No. 1 and Crosfield's No. 2 should have met on Saturday, but they evidently came to an arrangement, and No. 2 team retired. Crosfield's No. 1 therefore enter the second stage unopposed.

To-day the following teams will meet :—Orford Tannery v. Naylor's Timber Works; Howley Tannery v. Smith's Wire Works; Greening's Wire Works N 7.. Whitecross No. 3. Orford Tannery obtained a good position last year, and should stand a very good chance in to-day's engagement. It would be difficult to fore- cast the results of the other matches, as all the teams
are well drawh. There should be a rem, Close contest between Howley Tannery and Smith's tire Works:,

The Warrington and District League matches are arousing much interest and there were four games on Saturday. Bull's Head triumphed over Penketh Park by an 83 majority, winning no fewer than eleven- games out of the twelve. The closest contest Wag'. between A.. Shaw and A.. Higham, Shaw winning by 15 to 13. Brooklands tried conclusi ins with Fearn,- head, and gained the victory by 31. They had the best of -ten of the twelve games. R. Healey and IL Rowles were well matched, Healey winning by one point. Chapel House defeated Horse and Jockey bY 41, eight of the games being in their favour. j- Goulden had only a majority of one in his game with - A. Shelmerdine. The Liberal Club had to admit de— feat to the extent of 63 points at the hands of they Cemetery. Club who won ten games. There were - keenly fought contests between R. Rothwell and R- Marrow, Joseph Harrison and fl. Daintith, W. Hill and A. J. Jones, the victor in each case having a- ' majority of two.

Aic INTERESTING BOWLING HANDICAP. Hearing that the concluding stages of a successfut main were being contested at the King and Queell-' P3dgate, on Wednesday night (the first roundS having been played on Whit Monday) I decided to: witness the games, and I may say at once that I never witnessed better bowling than was exhibited by the players who took part. Most of the games were - closely contested, so closely in act that many result&. hung in the balance till the last wood was sent. Th final game (15 up), was between John Monks and John Jolley, two very good bowlers indeed. Both. were on the one mark. Jolley went away with a rush- and scored nine chalks to Monks three, making the game ten-four • in favour of Jolley. Monks then scored four to Jolley's three and the . game stood thirteen-eight in Jolley's favour. Everyone thought the contest was over, and to all appearances it was, but Monks, playing in irresistible- fashion, caught his man up at thirteen. Each novr wanted to two win. Monks led the Jack on his favourite mark, andplayed a wood about a foot wide of it, a very good bowl indeed, but still lying in a good position for Jolley to score off. This he tried to do, missing by the merest trifle, and just running out- Monks played another good wood, lying up for game, with Jolley one wood in hand. Jolley's move here was to run the Jacks if possible and make two of it; and playing with good judgment he sent his wood. ' Amidst () i Teat excitement t was seen that he had hit the object, but he had hard luck in not catching it quite full, leaving Monks a very popular winner by• two. The other prize winners were:—Torn Hackett,:• third, Peter Ball and J. W. Wor4ley, fourth and fifth. The conduct on the green was eAmplary, and credit is due to the landlord, Mr. Fred Clare, wlin i very' popular with both players and specta.„,-., of th-e' trundling art.

Cycling. The hopes of the wheelers who had looked forward to a first-class week-end for Whitsuntide touring were unfortunately not realised. Although Friday was an- ideal day, Saturday morning broke dull and unpro- mising and during the day there were heavy showers. Sunday :was dull but the rain kept off. Monday - morning was brilliantly fine and hundreds of cyclists - were to be seen enjoying themselves in Cheshire. A-. shower about eleven o'clock gave rise to alarm, alio- in the afternoon the rain set in steadily and did not clear off until about five o'c!ock-. Later in the. even- ing there were more showers.

The Warrington Club's touring pa,ty numbered ten, and the outlook; was net by any means encouraging.: when a start was made for Ellesmere and Lla-ngollent The tourists went by train to Crewe, and then pedalled on via Nantwich and Whitchurch to Ellesmere,wh.cre, I am told, a jolly night was spent at the good hostelry the Red Lion. On Sunday th machines/ were-- again brought up,and after a pleasant run via Whitting- ton Oswestry was reached for lunch, which lips duly provided at the Queens. Afterwards the party cycled through Chirk to Llangollen. Owing to the rain , which fell heavily at intervals the roads got in an- atrocious state, and side-slips were numerous. How- - ever. the wheelers arrived at Llangollen in time for a' good tea and a pleasant evening was spent at tbe,, - favourite resort of Warringtonians—the " On Monday the homeward journey was commenced, - and although the roads were heavy la places and there were smart showers, the run was accomplished without mishap. On the whole; thR tour was greatly enjoyed and formed a very pleosant change from the ordinary club ran. No doubt .if the-. weather is more favourable, a large number of meal-- bers will take advantage of the next holiday tour.

On Tuesday evening ths Warringtou 0.0. had the& usual club .run to Bucklow Hill. The.conditioas weret rather threatening at the outset, but the captain 311,1 eleven members turned out. The roads were 'l2' excellent order after the recent rains and the ride out was most agreeable. A few games of bowls wero. played on the green attached to the Swan, and after short stay for refreshments, the cyclists had a' glorious moonlight). ride home.
To-day's run is to Chester; lighting up time 9.2.1 On Tuesday evening the members visit the ancieol castle at Halton ; lighting up time, 9.25.

The destination of the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan' Cycling Club on Whit Monday was Macclesfield and, 16 members turned out. A start. was made at 9 o'clock- and before going 100 yards, one member had the mis— fortune to get a puncture. This caused a delay aneo: at Bank Quay a further stoppage was caused through a female member skidding on the tram lines. However Macclesfield was reached at 12.30 when dinner Wag provided by Mrs. Hood, 21, Prestbury-road. After dinner the party visited several parks and ars° the Derbyshire Hills. A start was made for home at s• o'clock,Warrington being reached after a most succesi: ful run just before 9 o clock.

div.head: Athletic Successes.
div.p: Athletic Successes.

Warrington athletes were fairly among the prize 9. during the holiday week end, no less than 16 trophies' of one sort or another being secured at various sports.. The old town can generally hold its own in the sport— ing world, and a few years ago Warrington athlete were always to the fore. Until just lately the nes!: generation has been rather quiet, hut the riders an runners of to-day are rapidly climbing the ladder of farad, and bid fair to uphold the best traditions of the district.

, At the Bury Police sports on Saturday, the follow— ing members of the Warrington A.thletic Club were' successful.: H. Alounfield, Ist Mile cycle, 185 yards B. Gornall, 3rd, 185 yards ; C. Berry, 2nd: half mile cycle, GO yards.

-- At Pontefract sports on Saturday a couple or Sankey Harriers and A.C. men men were ,showing th - way to their opponents. John Riley, 115 yards, toot the mile fiat race, and A. E. Howard secured thir& place in the mile cycle.

Quite a sheaf of awards fell to Warrington cyclists, at Castleford on Monday. H. Mounfield won both the 1 and 2 mile cycle races; 0. Berrey was third in the 2 miles, second in the half mile, and third in the' mile.

At Bangor C.C. sports on Monday, C. J. Straw cacae., first in the mile flat race from the GO yards mark, an," second from the 100 yards mark in the three 11 flat race, while Walter Collin annexed the honours ith both the 1 and 2 mile cycle races, and the mile' ".roadster."
At Lancaster on Tuesday, W. Price was second iEL the 2 mile walking handicap.

div.head: Football.
div.p: Football.

The railway companies have made an itnportan concession to football clubs, which should go a lou,t way towards reducing their travelling expenses. has been agreed that if excursion trains be run , connection with football matches, the players and cluu officials should be allowed to travel on the same dal by ordinary trains both ways at excursion train rate.: upon application by the secretary of the club. Thl is the result of a deputation of the Football League and other bodies which waited upon the rail, managers at the Clearing House, London, in Februnr. last.

A new definition of a gentlemen was given recently by the plaintiff in an ection brought in a eounty court. The defendant was described in the different sets of papers as a butcher, a builder, and a tailor. The judge finally appealed to the plaintiff, who replied: "Well, he is more like a gentleman than anything else. He walks about all day doing nothing, going from public-house to public-house." Having distin- guished himself in an unusual degree during a gathering of the clergy to an afternoon tea at the bishop's palace, he was taken to task for his fail- ings by a senior curate, who was one of his corn- panions on the way home. "Look here, Bruce," said the senior decidedly, "you are a donkey! Why cannot you keep quiet instead of making your asinine remarks? I am speaking to you now as' a brother—" Loud laughter interrupted him at this point,, and for the moment he wondered why.

If we stud when we want more' their interests, I feel sure About we can always get it. • -410.- W A RFAvi N GTO N S MAY PARADE. -CREDITABLE DISPLAY. vitike there was nothing in Warrington's May 'paraae of horses to mark specifically the " merrie 'month," the display on Saturday was distinctly Creditable to the town. The well-cared for and smartly-groomed horses which made a procession about a mile long showed that the committee's efforts to encourage drivers to take a kindly interest in their charges are being • attended with success. Public interest in the event—which already runs high— would, we believe, be increased if more in the way of Inovelty and picturesque effects were introduced next year. The parade would certainly gain in attractive- ness, and the probability is that the sum realized for local charities would Ile larger. The committee had done all in their power to make Saturday's parade a oomplete success. They had gone to the trouble .)f arranging a later date than usual, in the hope of being favoured with congenial weather conditions. They were doomed to disappoint- ment, for whilst the judging was in progress drizzling rain Tell, and did not cease until the procession was on its way. A. large field at Arpley—eminently suited for the purpose—was used as a judging ground. As may be readily imagined the almost uniform excellence of the turnouts made discrimination by no means easy, but the judge's awards appeared to meet with approval It is worthy of nate that very few hoNes failed to earn commendation. Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall showed their interest in the work by attending, and before the processionists left the ground,Lady Greenall presented the cups, medals and certificates to the successful competitors. A. hearty vote of thanks was accorded to her on the proposition of Mr. J. FULTON Sum the hon. treasurer, who remarked that the fact of 'Lady Greenall presenting the prizes was very encouraging to them, and he hoped that next year they would have the pleasure of seeing her ladyship again in the same position. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Lady GETENALL, in reply, -said she could assure all present tlhat it gave her very great pleasure to be present. She was very much pleased to see such 'excellent turnouts. She 'thought they were a great improvement on last year, and she hoped that next year there wquld be Still further improvement, and that all who had not won prizes this year would be more lucky at the next parade. (Hear, hear.) Forennately the rain 'cleared off soon after the parade commenced, and the route was well lined with. spectators. Of the parade itself, the shortest descrip- tion would be t, say -that it was practically the same as last year's. The entries for competition numbered 120—a slight increase upon 1903. It was noted that neither the railway companies nor Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and 'Co. were represented. First cane the Warrrington Fire Brigade, in charge of Superintendent Turner, with their brightly burnished helmets and artistically decorated .engines. The police ambulance made a smart turnout, and it was followed by Walker's Brewery Band resplendent in gold and green uniforms. Messrs. Peter Walker and Son's horses next arrested attention, and. fine, powerful creatures they were. In order that there should be no impression that corn- petition'was being'in any way restricted the firm did not enter for the cups or medals. The fifteen sections into which the parade was divided included many and widely vaned classes of horses. There were the heavy draught horses used by the manufacturers and in the Corporation departments; and the smart, light horses which draw tradesmen's vehicles. All were gaily caparisoned, and a toss of the head would set bells a-jingling. Mr. T. H. Houghton showed a •veteran horse with the homely name of "Robin," , which despite its 30 years, is still working every day, and from all appearances seems equal to another 30 , years' work. Messrs. Crosfields' Fire Brigade, under SuperintendenCGallon, made a brave show, and the beautiful decoration of the engine earned general praise. Four bands,—Walker's, Crosfield's, War- rington Borough and the Pioneer—discoursed lively music. As the procession passed along, the spectators were afforded an opportunity of helping on the work of two deserving institutions— the Infirmary and District Nursing AssociatiOn. The services of a large band of collectors had beenl enlisted, and-there were several vehicles decorated and specially arranged for the reception of coins. A. good harvest of coppers was forthcoming, and the collection totalled about £3O 2s. 9s. which will be divided between the institutions. The following route was traversed :—Parker-street, Sankey-street, Buttermarket-street, Church-street, round the Lamp- Church-street, Mersey-street, Bridge- street, Horsemarket-street, Winwick-street, Tanners- lane, Froghall-lane, Priestley-street, Powys-street, Bank Quay, Sankey-street, Bold-street and Wilson Patten- street.
